title: Fraser named Carlton coach after leading Blues' AFL revival
text:
Carlton chief executive Graham Wright insists Josh Fraser's presentation alone would have been enough to guarantee his appointment as senior coach.

After a fairytale rise from 1-8 when Michael Voss exited as coach, Fraser was the unanimous choice to steer the Blues forward.

The former Collingwood and Gold Coast ruckman has won 10 of 13 games to guide Carlton into the most unlikely of finals appearances.

Sunday's draw against the Western Bulldogs sealed Carlton's spot in the top 10, with the club's board meeting to finalise Fraser's appointment on Monday.

Loading Instagram content

The results gave him the edge on untried assistants Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong), who all loomed strongly and presented to the coaching panel before Fraser did.

"Even if you removed the last 14 weeks, on his presentation alone Josh would have been the successful candidate," Wright said.

"Having run all candidates through a thorough and detailed process, for Josh to have emerged as the stand-out candidate speaks volumes of not only his credentials as a coach, but also the qualities he brings as a leader.

"He is a respectful whole-of-club leader who fosters a professional and united environment, with everyone contributing to our collective pursuit of excellence."

Even though he spent the majority of his playing career at the Magpies, Fraser's coaching journey has been largely at the old enemy.

The 44-year-old has had two stints as an assistant coach at Carlton, while also leading the club's VFL team.

When becoming interim coach, Fraser immediately ruled himself out of contention to stay in the role next year as a way to take pressure off the club.

"I have always had ambitions to be a senior coach and what the last three months have done is give me the absolute belief that I am ready, and most importantly ready for this exact opportunity, to be senior coach of the Carlton football club," Fraser said.

"When I was told that I had been appointed as senior coach, that sense of appreciation and responsibility I felt in that moment will never be lost on me.

"I firmly believe I am a product of amazing people around me.

"The collective commitment to each other and to get better every day in order to improve our football club is a privilege to be part of, and rest assured we want to continue to raise the standards in that regard."

AAP

title: Labor prepared to fast-track fix to negative gearing 'widow tax'
text:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the government is prepared to fast-track a fix to the unintended "widow tax" created by its changes to negative gearing if it will win the Coalition's support to save $37 billion in NDIS spending.

The Coalition is supportive of the massive savings package for the NDIS but has remained in negotiations with the government on the bill, which Labor hopes to pass this week.

Yesterday, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor issued the government an ultimatum for its support on the NDIS: Fix the "cruel" loophole unintentionally cutting off home owners from negative gearing if their partner dies or they separate due to family violence.

Property investors are still able to claim rental losses on their income tax, known as negative gearing, if the home was bought or settled before budget night.

But the government's tax changes announced in May introduced an unintended consequence for co-owners of an investment property that meant if one of them died, the partner who inherited their share of the property would lose the ability to negatively gear it, since it now counted as a new ownership for tax purposes.

Independent senator David Pocock identified the "widow tax" as the negative gearing changes were passed through the Senate with the support of the Greens, calling for it to be abolished as a matter of urgency since it was already preventing individuals from securing financing.

Senator Pocock has raised the case of a woman who left her partner due to family violence, and was now unable to secure a bank loan to refinance her investment property that she co-owned with the former partner since it would no longer be eligible for negative gearing after July next year.

The federal government has introduced draft legislation that would fix the loophole as part of a second tranche of housing tax reforms. However, that bill was not expected to be dealt with this fortnight.

This morning, Mr Chalmers said the government was willing to negotiate a fast-tracked fix to the widow tax in order to win the Coalition's support on its massive NDIS savings package.

"The government has already made it abundantly clear, crystal clear, that we are addressing some of those issues raised in that draft legislation that I put out some time ago, and that we have consulted on," Mr Chalmers said.

"Now, if the opposition's main ask is that we pass the government's legislation quicker, then obviously I'm up for that discussion."

Mr Chalmers said he would not detail negotiations with the opposition, which he said were primarily being held between the prime minister and opposition leader.

title: Rugby league State of Origin headed to New Zealand for first time
text:
Australian rugby league's showpiece event will head across the Tasman for the first time, with the men's State of Origin confirmed for Auckland next year.

The Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) announced on Tuesday that Game II of the 2027 series will be played at Auckland's Eden Park.

It will be only the second time State of Origin has been played outside Australia, with California hosting a match in 1987 at Veterans Memorial Stadium, which was won by the Blues 30–18.

ARLC chairman Peter V’landys said the Origin match, scheduled for June 16, 2027, will be part of a wider rugby league festival in New Zealand's largest city.

"State of Origin is truly unique. It creates an atmosphere unlike anything else in Australian sport — fierce rivalry, raw passion and an intensity that can only be understood by experiencing it firsthand. It's a bucket-list event," Mr V'landys said.

"It's not just the Origin match fans can look forward to — we are planning a week of rugby league festivities in the lead-up to the event, starting with a Warriors game at Eden Park on the Sunday afternoon prior to the Origin fixture.

"It's going to be a complete takeover of Auckland, showcasing the best of our game to New Zealanders and fans travelling from all over the world."

Despite being a contest between Queensland and New South Wales, the State of Origin series has garnered widespread interest since its inception in 1980.

Eligibility rules were changed this year to allow some players to represent Queensland or New South Wales, but then be selected for New Zealand and England in the Test area.

Kalyn Ponga, Addin Fonua-Blake and Briton Nikora all played in this year's Origin series and will be available for Kiwi selection at this year's World Cup.

title: Maroons' search for new Origin coach suffers double setback
text:
Billy Slater's old pair of assistants in Matt Ballin and Ben Te'o loom as the two leading candidates to take over as Queensland coach, after Cameron Smith and Kevin Walters ruled themselves out of the race.

In a seismic Monday night for Maroons State of Origin officials, Smith first pulled out of the running.

The champion hooker had been the early frontrunner to replace Slater, who had publicly backed him to do a "fantastic job" if handed the job.

Billy Slater to step down as Maroons' head coach The 43-year-old, who oversaw five State or Origin series with Queensland, says he will not stay in the role for 2027.

Queensland captain Cameron Munster and Wayne Bennett had also endorsed Smith as the man to take over, before the 43-year-old ruled himself out of the role.

A little over 24 hours later, the state's most-capped player said it was not the time for him to take on a head-coaching role at the Maroons.

"I've heard comments from Wayne Bennett [endorsing me] and I really appreciate the sentiments, but it's not the role for me at this current time," Smith said on Nine's 100% Footy.

"I was lucky enough to be involved in the camp with the players and Billy when he started in 2022 and '23 and thoroughly enjoyed my time.

"But there was a reason I stepped away after 2023. I couldn't fully commit to the role and at the time that was an assistant coach, not head coach.

"And nothing in my life has changed."

There had also been conjecture that Walters could stand down from his post as Australia's Test coach after the World Cup and return to the Maroons.

Walters coached Queensland to two series wins during his stint in charge between 2016 and 2019 and would have had arguably the best resume of all candidates.

But he too confirmed to News Corp last night he would not be taking on the Maroons job, vowing to honour his two-year deal as Kangaroos coach.

That leaves Queensland officials with a search for Slater's replacement.

Ballin now shapes as a likely frontrunner, having served as Slater's assistant since 2023.

Matt Ballin is considered to be an option for the Maroons to be the next coach. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

The 42-year-old played an Origin for the Maroons in 2010 and was a leading option for the full-time job at Manly this year before Kieran Foran's hot start.

He has been on Brisbane's staff since 2021, and is highly regarded in Queensland.

Te'o has also served as an assistant to Slater and had held a similar role to Ballin on Brisbane's staff before his high-profile exit earlier this year.

The back-rower played seven games for Queensland between 2012 and 2014, and was in charge of the Broncos' defence through last year's premiership run.

Slater's other key member of staff, Johnathan Thurston, has already ruled himself out of the running.

Josh Hannay is another who long served on the Maroons coaching staff, but it is understood Gold Coast would be unlikely to allow him to juggle Titans and Queensland duties.

Anthony Seibold has also spent time as a Maroons assistant and could shape as another option.

AAP

title: Queensland graziers pushed to the brink as feed runs dry
text:
For the first time in his 28-year career, Greg Finlay's hay sheds are empty.

Mr Finlay, a 58-year-old mixed cattle and crop farmer near Texas, a small Queensland border town about 300 kilometres south-west of Brisbane, said he had always managed to keep bales in stock.

Greg Finlay walks through one of his empty hay sheds. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

But the prolonged period of below-average rainfall was starting to bite for much of the region.

Much of southern Queensland, which includes an area roughly twice the size of Belgium, has been drought declared for the first time in two years.

Queensland entered its last major drought in 2013, with areas of the state remaining drought-stricken until 2024.

Map of drought declared regions of south-west Queensland as of August 1, 2026. (Supplied: Queensland Government)

For many, those years in drought still run deep.

The impacted area includes the Balonne, Goondiwindi, Southern Downs and parts of Maranoa, where some primary producers have begun to sell their animals.

"There've been people destocking for a while now as the drought's worn on," Mr Finlay said.

For the first time in Greg Finlay's career, all of his hay sheds are empty. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

He said others have put their animals on agistment further south where conditions were more favourable.

It comes as the Bureau of Meteorology's climate outlook for September suggests below-average rainfall could be experienced across the south and east of the nation and daytime temperatures are likely to be above average south of the tropics.

Mr Finlay said his property had received 167 millimetres of rain for the year so far, compared to a 650mm annual rainfall average.

Four councils in Queensland were fully or partly drought declared in July 2026. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

He said it meant he had only been able to produce about 40 per cent of the hay he usually would, and producers were shipping hay in from Victoria, South Australia and north Queensland to feed their animals.

Mr Finlay said the memories of the recent drought between 2012 and 2020 remained fresh.

He said there was only 30 per cent of the livestock left by the end of the eight years.

A dry paddock near Surat in south-west Queensland, following the drought declaration. (ABC Southern Qld: Bella Munro)

"I think there's probably a lot of PTSD and people are worried about this," he said.

"They don't trust that these are short-lived events.

"We are noticing extremes in what happens with our climates, extreme wet, extreme dry."

River stops running

Further inland near the outback town of Surat, grazier Keith Allwood works on several properties in the Maranoa and St George regions and said most of the cattle farmers he knew were all feeding their cattle because there was very little to graze on.

Keith Allwood works on several properties across the Balonne Shire and the Maranoa. (ABC Southern Qld: Bella Munro)

"It's not just the stock, it's the farmers. They haven't got the rain to plant, or if they did plant, some of the crops just come to nothing," he said.

"It will take a long time for the feed to come back."

One of the region's major rivers, the Balonne River, recently stopped running and Mr Allwood said it was the first time in more than five years.

"It'll be bad, and the dryer it gets, the harder it's going to be to get feed," he said.

Impacts on local wildlife

Wildlife are having to travel further in search of food and water. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Wildlife carers are also struggling with an influx of animals as nearby creeks dry up and food sources become more scarce.

Wildlife Empire Rescue and Rehabilitation in Inglewood, north-west of Texas, rescues injured and orphaned wildlife.

The centre's director, Tennille Bankes, said they were seeing more kangaroos injured on roads as they travelled further to find food and water.

She said it was getting harder by the week to care for the animals, as there was no access to hay in the area.

Tennille Bankes is worried about how to feed animals in her care. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

With limited access to feed, staff have had to go out and pick their own hay and grass.

"We're very, very concerned about the impacts of the drought," she said.

"When the land isn't providing for the animals, we're having to provide for the animals."

Fire threat

Scrubby Creek Rural Fire Brigade volunteers conducting a hazard-reduction burn in the Goondiwindi region. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Rural fire brigades have been conducting hazard-reduction burns in preparation for the upcoming bushfire season, as the dry conditions pose a potential risk.

Scrubby Creek Rural Fire Brigade volunteer Dennis Dwyer said crews had less time to conduct hazard-reduction burns after a long, hot summer season.

"This year was a shorter window by far, and it's going to close very soon, I imagine," he said.

Volunteers Helen and Dennis Dwyer conducting a hazard reduction burn in the Millmerran region in south-west Queensland. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

title: Stress-free Book Week costumes with a musical twist
text:
Across Australia, the Children's Book Week parade with its costume displays is a cherished and sometimes dreaded tradition for generations of parents and kids.

This year, there's a musical twist to the theme: Symphony of Stories.

We talk to musically inclined parents, an author and an ABC Classic presenter to get ideas on how your kids can take part in the Symphony of Stories.

They also share tips on how to take some of the stress out of Book Week costume crafting.

Choosing books about music

ABC Classic presenter Danielle McGrane reads stories to her children every night.

"It's part of the ritual of going to bed," McGrane says.

For families looking to embrace this year's Symphony of Stories theme, books inspired by music can offer both reading inspiration and costume ideas.

McGrane's collection includes stories inspired by classical music, such as Carnival of the Animals and The Planets, which she's currently reading with her child.

"The Planets is a book about young explorers going to all the different planets and there's a little button that can be pressed to play the music from Gustav Holst's The Planets," she says.

Book Week celebrates the simple joy of reading, says Danielle McGrane. (ABC Classic: Lucy Zee)

Musical storybooks can be a great way to introduce young children to different instruments and composers.

"I've been reading and playing Carnival of the Animals with my kids from quite a young age," McGrane says.

"There are so many book versions of this story. And what it does is give instruments like the cello or the tuba a personality that kids can relate to."

Other books, such as The Flying Orchestra, can show children that "music is a tool for emotional expression," McGrane says.

Books like these can provide simple inspiration for Symphony of Stories costumes.

McGrane has some tips for parents who are anxious about jazzing up their costume game: "Pick two costumes you feel you can achieve, and offer your child the choice between those two."

Whether you're dressing your child as an animal from Carnival of the Animals or an instrument from The Flying Orchestra, McGrane says "the important thing is to feel the link between the story and the music."

Choosing books with musical connections

Blue Mountains author Jodie McLeod feels differently about Book Week, depending on which hat she's wearing.

"As an author, I can't wait to share my love of books with schools and students, but as a parent, I'm nervous," she says.

One of McLeod's books, Leonard the Lyrebird, has been inspiring Book Week costumes since it was published in 2018.

McLeod has seen children dress up as lyrebirds, which are famed for their mimicking abilities and impressive performances in the Australian bush.

"They would be wearing greys and browns, carrying some feathers and props with musical notes," she shares.

Author and parent Jodie McLeod has mixed feelings about Book Week depending on which hat she's wearing. (Supplied: Jodie McLeod)

Those musical touches feel especially fitting because Leonard the Lyrebird has found a second life as a stage musical, joining a long tradition of books that have been adapted for new audiences, from Gumnut Babies to Matilda.

McLeod says the boundaries between books, theatre and screen adaptations have become increasingly blurred, opening up even more possibilities for Book Week costumes.

"Tim Minchin's Matilda, for example, has a lot of iconic grey and white school uniforms with ties and blazers, and there's a lot of gorgeous choreography in that musical."

McLeod says practicality and cooperation of her kids are the deciding factors for Book Week.

The Book Week parade also gives teachers a chance to rock their costumes. (Supplied: Jodie McLeod)

As a parent of older children on the cusp of their teenage years, she has to take their likes and dislikes into account.

"My children have never been very inclined to wear elaborate costumes to school," McLeod admits.

"The best costumes have been those where my kids can dress up mostly as themselves, but have some feature or prop that distinguishes them as a character from a book."

This approach might be handy for families learning a musical instrument, especially one that's easy to carry.

For parents who don't have the time, budget or enthusiasm for elaborate costume-making, McLeod points out there's another way to embrace this year's musical theme: "incorporate some singing and dancing into the Book Week parade".

Find musical elements in books you already have

Book Week is the highlight of Ballarat-based mum of four Deneale Deppeler's year.

"I do love dressing up as a way to express my creativity through Book Week," Deppeler says.

Book Week is the highlight of the year for Ballarat-based mum of four Deneale Deppeler. (Supplied: Deneale Deppeler)

She even organises a Book Week version of trick-or-treating on her street, called "Books n' Bon Bons".

"I get a lot of joy out of it, but I know not everybody will feel the same," she says.

Deppeler is strict about ensuring her children dress up as characters from books rather than "just any TV characters".

Deneale Deppeler loves a bit of ceremony and an occasion to dress up. (Supplied: Deneale Deppeler)

But Deppeler says getting on board with this year's Symphony of Stories theme is easier than parents might think.

"Music might not always be in the front seat of a storybook, but you'll often find musical elements hidden throughout stories, even if it's not the main thing."

That means parents don't have to start with an obviously musical book to embrace the theme.

Deppeler points to popular favourites including Grug, Peter Rabbit, Paddington Bear and Ruby Red Shoes as potential sources of inspiration.

To keep Book Week as stress-free as possible, Deppeler has a few costume-making rules of her own, including deciding what costumes her kids will wear.

The aim is to create costumes using materials already in the house and items from her children's wardrobes.

Some of the examples Deppeler suggests include making cardboard cut-outs of a violin, or using a paper towel roll to create a clarinet or a microphone.

"This is where my creativity comes in," Deppeler says. "I just need a shoe box and some folding paper and bam, I've got an accordion; a Milo tin makes a drum."

Deppeler creates costumes mainly using items from around the house and her children's wardrobes. (Supplied: Deneale Deppeler)

Many popular children's stories, including Grug, feature musical elements between its pages. (Supplied: Deneale Deppeler)

Deppeler also recommends reusing costumes from previous Book Week parades.

"If you've got a bear costume from Paddington Bear, there's no reason why you shouldn't reuse it for stories like The Very Noisy Bear, which is about trying out different musical instruments," she says.

Ultimately, Deppeler says the most important thing about Book Week is "getting kids to become passionate about reading and discovering what other people are reading through their costumes."

ABC Classic celebrates Children's Book Week from Saturday 22 — Friday 28 August, exploring the connection between literature, imagination and classical music.

title: Hockeyroos downed by reigning champions in World Cup pool match
text:
The Hockeyroos have been beaten by the Netherlands in their second match of the FIH Hockey World Cup, going down 4-2 despite a battling performance against the reigning champions.

Australia are nevertheless well placed to qualify for the second round with the group's other result going their way.

Rejuvenated Hockeyroos and Kookaburras tackle World Cup with fresh perspectives The Kookaburras and Hockeyroos' last major tournament was Paris 2024 where they exited in the quarter-finals. They have both experienced significant change since then, and are determined to start their new eras with success at the World Cup.

The Aussies took Monday's game to their hosts from the opening whistle in the Amsterdam suburb of Amstelveen, producing a strong first quarter and putting the world number one team under sustained pressure.

The Hockeyroos earned a startling eight penalty corners in the opening term, including seven in succession, but were unable to find the breakthrough.

Australia paid for their profligacy as the Dutch showed them how it is done, scoring with their first penalty corner through Yibbi Jansen in the 13th minute.

The Netherlands doubled their advantage in contentious circumstances.

Australia referred Joosje Burg's goal for a potential back stick in the build-up, with replays showing the ball had made contact with the back of a Dutch stick. However, because the incident occurred outside the attacking 23-metre area, it was deemed non-referable, and the goal stood.

Refusing to let the setback halt their momentum, the Hockeyroos continued to attack and were eventually rewarded through Steph Kershaw, who found the back of the net in the 23rd minute to reduce the deficit.

Kershaw was involved again as Australia drew level at 2-2, getting the faintest of touches on an Abi Williams flick to set up a thrilling finish against the tournament favourites.

With the match in the balance heading into the final quarter, the Netherlands showed why they are the world's top-ranked side.

The Dutch piled pressure on the Australian defence, earning five penalty corners in the final quarter, scoring twice in the space of four minutes through Burg and Marjin Veen to take control of Group A.

The Hockeyroos now turn their attention to Chile on Wednesday from 5:30pm, AEST.

Chile are pointless having lost 3-0 to Japan.

With Australia beating Japan 2-0 in their opening game, a Hockeyroos victory will ensure their progress to the next stage, unless Japan unexpectedly beat the Dutch. In that case, goal difference will come into play so Australia will be seeking a large win over the South Americans.

title: Live: BHP reports 30pc profit jump on high copper prices
text:
My great colleague Stephen Letts yesterday compiled a week-ahead look. Key among it: wages and jobs updates

Australia:

Tue: Consumer sentiment (Aug) Wed: Wage Price Index (Q2) RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser speaks Thu: Employment/unemployment (Jul) Inflation expectations (Aug)

International:

Mon: CN — Retail sales, Industrial production, Fixed asset investment (Jul) JP — GDP (Q2) Tue: US — Building permits, Housing starts (Jul), Industrial production (Jul) Wed: US — FOMC minutes UK — CPI (Jul) Fri: Global — PMIs for US, EU, UK, JP

This week's macro focus at home will be on wages and jobs.

Last week we had the ABS's Average Weekly Earnings (AWE) data that showed wages had risen 0.8% over the quarter, 3.7% over the year.

This week the ABS trots out its quarterly Wage Price Index (WPI).

There are subtle differences between the two measures. Here's the ABS's handy guide to both.

AWE measures average gross weekly earnings paid to employees and reflects real-world changes in both the level of earnings per employee and in the composition of employment. AWE is used if the focus is on understanding changes in the level of average earnings over time.

WPI measures the price change in wages and salaries over time, focusing on wage inflation and inflationary pressures associated with wages and salaries. It follows changes in the hourly rate paid to a fixed group of jobs and does not reflect changes in location where work is performed. The WPI is useful for understanding wage growth trends in the Australian labour market.

In other words, The WPI is more focused on the price change of wages, while the AWE provides a broader view of earnings growth.

Westpac is forecasting the WPI to have increased at around 0.8% over the quarter, similar to Q1.

That would see the WPI tick down from an annual pace of 3.3% to 3.2%. That would be below the CPI (Consumer Price Index) which was running closer to 4% in the year to May.

Looking ahead, Westpac notes the Fair Work Commission's 2026 Annual Wage Review handed down a larger-than-expected increase in award wages of 4.75%. That will come into effect in Q3, which Westpac expects will raise the WPI pace back around the 3½%yr mark.

On Thursday, the ABS also trots out its monthly reading of Australia's labour market.

Job creation has been volatile, jumping a heady 73,000 in June.

Market economists are forecasting around 13,000 new jobs in July, although the range of guesses is pretty wide from 15,000 fewer jobs to a gain of 25,000.

A higher participation rate has put the unemployment rate under pressure, but it is expected to hold at around 4.4% in July.

Also this week, the always interesting RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser conducts another "fireside chat" (Tuesday). The RBA is seriously going to have to look at their carbon emissions with their penchant for fireside chats, even though summer, and maybe suggest those attending to just rug up.

Overseas, China's monthly economic data release out later today will be worth a look. We'll bring you numbers.

We'll also get a read of the Federal Reserve's rate setting committee's (FOMC) minutes on Wednesday and a take on global manufacturing via a variety of PMIs on Friday.

title: Mourners say Jason Arday 'was hunted' by tabloid media before his death
text:
Mourners at a London vigil for Jason Arday have accused the British tabloid media of "hunting" the late Cambridge professor, with thousands of people now calling for an inquiry into his death.

Professor Arday died last week following weeks of intense media coverage that questioned the veracity of his extraordinary life story and the provenance of his academic work.

The 41-year-old sociology professor, who made history in 2023 as Cambridge's youngest Black professor, had reportedly told friends his position at the fabled institution was constantly being undermined and university leadership have described the intense press reaction as a "racist feeding frenzy".

At a vigil organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism in Trafalgar Square, there was a feeling of immense sadness mixed with visceral anger toward the media.

One attendee told the ABC she believed Dr Arday was "hunted and hunted and hunted until the young man didn't have a choice".

Another mourner stated, "He was a Black man who beat all the odds and succeeded at Cambridge, an institution that we tell our young men to strive for. But he was hounded; it was a witch hunt".

One man described the last few days as "traumatic" as the UK's Black community processed Dr Arday's sudden passing.

Organisers estimated "several thousand" people attended the gathering.

More than 90,000 people have signed a petition seeking an independent inquiry into the media's handling of the academic.

The petition states his death followed "two weeks of relentless harassment".

The press scrutiny focused heavily on Dr Arday's claims he was non-verbal during his childhood, that he had achieved extraordinary athletic feats, and he had signed a lucrative book deal.

Much of the reporting also accused Dr Arday, whose core research revolved around race relations and inequality, of plagiarising his PhD thesis.

More than 90,000 people have signed a petition seeking an independent inquiry into the media's handling of the academic. (Reuters: Chris J Ratcliffe)

Cambridge Chancellor says possible to 'hold to two principles'

Cambridge Chancellor Lord Chris Smith said Dr Arday's treatment had crossed a line.

"I do believe it is possible to hold to two principles at the same time: to believe in the importance of academic integrity, and where criticisms of plagiarism arise about any academic, whoever they are, ensure that they are rigorously investigated," he said.

"And also to refuse to join in a racist feeding frenzy over a particular academic."

Dr Arday resigned from his post on August 5.

In his resignation letter, he emphasised his departure "should not be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

Following his death, a crowdfunding campaign raised more than $300,000 to support funeral costs and his wife and two children.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has declined to state whether the government will formally back a public inquiry described the professor's death as a "tragedy on every level".

title: Labour hire company and four farms face more than $3 million in fines
text:
The Victorian Labour Hire Authority (LHA) is today set to bring about its largest case against farms allegedly using unlicensed labour hire companies.

The regulator is prosecuting seven entities in the Victorian Supreme Court, including a Swan Hill-based labour hire company and four Victorian horticultural farms, over alleged breaches of the state's labour hire licensing laws.

If successful, the labour hire company and four farms could be fined up to $3.3 million, while two labour hire company owners could individually face fines of up to $160,000.

The LHA became aware of the alleged violations after it was tipped off about Soo Soo Siong Pty Ltd allegedly paying workers below the legal minimum rate under the Horticulture Award.

An investigation found the company was unlicensed between April 2023 and March 2024.

Four farms face allegations

During this time, it allegedly provided labour hire services to four farms: Cutri Fruit Trusco Pty Ltd, Infantino United Fruit Pty Ltd, Mallee Fresh Produce Pty Ltd and A & A Marra & Sons.

The four farms allegedly paid Soo Soo Siong Pty Ltd about $750,000 over 11 months for labour hire services.

The case also included allegations a Malaysian national was confined to a property and restaurant by Soo Soo Siong owners Kwai Chow Lee and Akhmar Salni Mohamad-Ramlee for more than three years.

The LHA alleged the man's name and passport were used without his knowledge or consent to open a bank account and apply for a labour hire licence for Soo Soo Siong.

Acting labour hire licensing commissioner Michelle Osborne said the case demonstrated why labour hire licensing was important.

"This case provides one of the best examples I've seen of why labour hire licensing matters," she said.

"We are talking about serious harm here, and serious money, and exactly the kinds of risks we've been highlighting to growers across Victoria for years now."

The Victorian regulator said it hoped targeted action against farms would be a significant deterrent for others.

The LHA made its first prosecution against a farm employing workers from an unlicensed company in March earlier this year.

Yarra Valley orchard Sanders Apples is alleged to have sourced workers to pick and pack apples through an unlicensed company between 2023 and 2024.

The case is still ongoing in the Supreme Court and the farm could face up to $650,000 in fines if found guilty.

Swan First Farming Services owner Sayed Mahdi, who runs a small labour hire company in Swan Hill, said it was frustrating to hear about other companies allegedly doing the wrong thing.

"[These] kinds of people shouldn't be in this business … they should do the right thing, just listen and don't put a bad name on other contractors," he said.

"This job is already too hard … especially now with these kinds of things happening and then there is more pressure coming … it's very hard to handle."

Mr Mahdi has run his company for seven years but, due to the pressures of sourcing workers and tight industry regulations, said he would not remain in the industry for much longer.

The four farms allegedly involved could face up to $670,000 each in fines. (ABC Mildura-Swan Hill: Wade Stephens)

National authority needed

The case has also reignited industry conversations calling for a national labour hire authority.

Citrus Australia chief executive Nathan Hancock said the horticultural industry had been calling for a national labour hire licence scheme for a number of years.

"I think in situations where there's regulation in some parts of the industry and nothing in others, it just leads to opportunistic people taking advantage of others in the lesser situations," Mr Hancock said.

He said the citrus industry operators in the Sunraysia region were subject to inconsistent regulation either side of the Murray River.

"In Victoria there is a labour hire authority, but then you've got New South Wales, literally across the river, has no rules at all," he said.

"We see a lot of the Phoenix-type operations that are here one day and gone the next happening in New South Wales and it's a real let-down."

The Victoria Labour Hire Licensing Authority was established in 2019 after the state government passed the Labour Hire Licensing Act the year prior.

In the seven years since the authority's inception, it has collected close to $4 million in penalties through over a dozen prosecutions and cancelled just over 1000 licences.

In South Australia, the Consumer and Business Services is the authority responsible for labour hire licensing.

However, New South Wales has no labour hire licensing regulator.

"A lot of our industry is along a river system, and we have businesses that have crops in multiple states, so having different approaches to employment in all of these areas is a problem that we could erase with the national labour hire licensing scheme," Mr Hancock said.

title: LIV Golf ending season early after cancelling final event
text:
LIV Golf is ending its season one week earlier than planned, announcing on Monday it will not hold the team championship in Michigan next week and instead crown the team champion this week.

The 12 events this year — New Orleans was previously postponed — are the smallest schedule for LIV since it was launched with massive Saudi Arabian funding and eight tournaments in 2022.

Jon Rahm has already clinched the individual season title for the third straight year. LIV Golf Indianapolis, which starts on Thursday at The Club at Chatham Hills, will determine who finishes second and third among the players, and the top team.

Embattled LIV Golf tour asks to defer payment to Adelaide golf club The future of LIV Golf Adelaide has been further "shrouded in doubt", the SA opposition says, after LIV asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club, which is scheduled to host the event next year.

The Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, the financial muscle of the rival league from the start, decided in March this would be the final year of funding.

LIV Golf announced earlier this month it had an agreement with a lead investor that would sustain a new version of the league for 2027.

"By concluding the season now, we can put our full resources behind what comes next and maintain the operational rigor this transition demands," LIV CEO Scott O'Neil said in a statement.

"We are reimagining LIV Golf as a fundamentally new league owned by the players and anchored in a sustainable business model, with an evolved fan experience built for the markets where the game is growing fastest across the globe and the support of world-class partners."

The cancellation of LIV Golf Michigan was not surprising.

There have been reports in recent weeks the tournament had not even started preparing with grandstands and other amenities. LIV Golf said ticket holders would get refunds.

In another cost-cutting move LIV attributed to "unavoidable changes in the entertainment program", the league informed Thomas Rhett and Disco Lines their live performances would not take place at LIV Golf Indianapolis.

The final event, with a $US20 million ($28.1 million) purse that pays $US4 million to the winner, could be the last big pay-off for LIV and its 57 players.

LIV did not identify the lead investor or how much of a cash infusion was involved, or say whether it was an investment or a loan.

O'Neil has said the LIV 2.0 version for 2027 and onward would involve making players equity owners. He referred to it as a "second bite at the apple" being equity instead of cash.

But this likely is the end of $US20 million purses for individual outcomes, and there have already been cutbacks. Rahm earned $US6 million for winning the points title, down from $US18 million the previous two years.

"As we concentrate on finishing the season strong and building the next chapter of LIV Golf, we'll carry the energy and enthusiasm our fans have shown us into what comes next," O'Neil said.

The format for the 2027 season and the rosters also remain unclear.

Still to be determined is whether Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau — the two biggest names — and other players who joined the league for its exorbitant prize money will want to stay for LIV 2.0.

As for the final event, Joaquin Niemann, Lucas Herbert and Tyrrell Hatton are in the mix for third place, which pays a $US1 million bonus. DeChambeau is comfortably in second, which pays $US3 million.

Dustin Johnson's 4Aces team has a narrow lead over Australia-based Ripper, with Rahm's Legion XIII and Bryson DeChambeau's Crushers team all in the mix for the team title.

title: Sydney Airport 'crisis' a 'long time coming', retired airline pilot says
text:
Sydney Airport could face "catastrophic" consequences if safety issues are not addressed, following three incidents in as many weeks, a former pilot and aviation safety investigator says.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) revealed last Thursday it was investigating a third mishap, this time involving a Qantas flight crossing the path of a departing Virgin Australia aircraft.

It said at 10am on August 9, Virgin flight VA555 to Perth had its clearance to take-off rescinded by air traffic control soon after it had been given.

It is understood Qantas flight QF728 began to cross the runway more than 1,200 metres away from the Virgin plane, after also receiving clearance.

Just three hours earlier, there was a near miss between a Jetstar plane and a Qatar Airways aircraft at the same airport.

A Jetstar cabin crew worker was injured when the A320 plane had to brake suddenly to avoid colliding with a Boeing 777 under tow.

Two weeks prior, on July 27, a Qantas Link flight and a Qantas plane were involved in a near-miss on the tarmac.

Geoff Klouth has 35 years of experience working with commercial airlines. (Supplied: Geoff Klouth)

Retired commercial airline pilot and former aviation safety inspector Geoff Klouth said if the safety issues were not rectified "quickly", a worse incident could occur.

"We've been very fortunate that there haven't been collisions, but it doesn't mean it won't happen in the future," he said.

"It's only luck preventing the aircraft coming together because the system is not working at present.

" I'll say that the chances from a risk management level … are high that something will happen and the consequences of that could be catastrophic. "

ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said on Friday there were "multiple lines of defence" in an emergency situation like the trio of recent incidents.

"I will say in all three instances, there was a layer of defence that kicked in and prevented an escalation," he said.

"We find in a lot of our investigations it is very rarely a single point of failure. For it to progress through to an actual accident, multiple things need to go wrong."

'Matter of significant interest'

The trio of incidents began with a near miss in late July. (ABC News)

Mr Klouth's aviation career spanned 35 years, making his way from flying instructor to piloting Kendell, Ansett and Qantas commercial airlines in Australia and overseas.

While mostly based at Melbourne Airport, he frequently flew in and out of Sydney.

He also spent 18 months as a senior aviation safety investigator at the ATSB, followed by a long stint with Jetstar as a first officer, fleet safety investigator, training captain and flight operations auditor from 2006 until he retired in 2023.

Mr Klouth said one of the reasons he retired was because the systems that used to support pilots were "diminishing in quality and standards".

He said this included a reduction in air traffic controllers employed by Airservices Australia, as well as procedures managed by airports and the regulatory Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA).

"You were expected to maintain a safe flight, but you weren't given the processes around it," Mr Klouth said.

Staffing issues are one reason Mr Klouth decided to retire. (Supplied: Geoff Klouth)

CASA did not answer questions sent by the ABC about safety systems, citing the current investigation.

However, the regulatory authority said the third incident was a "matter of significant interest" to them and it was working with Airservices Australia.

"It is important that we allow time for the ATSB to investigate this and the other incidents fully and that we do not prejudice its investigation by speculating on their cause," it said in a statement.

The ABC also contacted Sydney Airport for comment about safety issues and risks of a possible collision, to which it responded safety was and always would be "the first priority".

"Australia has one of the safest aviation systems in the world, supported by rigorous oversight from safety regulators, airlines, airports, and air navigation service providers," a spokesperson said.

Mr Klouth said Airservices Australia "tried to diminish" the latest runway incident by suggesting there was "still plenty of room".

"The point is that the system should be there, the procedures should be in place, so that never happens," he said.

Airservices Australia says it is working with the ATSB. (Supplied: Geoff Klouth)

Airservices Australia did not respond to Mr Klouth's allegation about safety measures and staffing levels, instead pointing to previous statements.

The company previously said safety was its top priority.

On Friday, CEO Rob Sharp said initial reviews of the recent incidents had not uncovered systemic issues compromising passenger safety.

He said the government body responsible for managing air traffic did not believe the incident met the threshold for reporting because an "experienced controller" rescinded clearance to the Virgin pilot immediately, the aircraft was stationary, and it was 1,300 metres from the Qantas plane.

"We do take our reporting requirements very seriously," he said.

"But we will work closely with the ATSB because there are some data points that need to be resolved and clarified … we look forward to any learnings that come from that particular incident."

'Structural challenge'

Mr Klouth said the Sydney Airport "crisis" was a "long time coming".

"I could see that [safety issues] already starting to happen due to staffing levels … but what we're seeing is the end result of that," he said.

"If one controller is busy doing multiple tasks or they've been called in to come into work on multiple days off, fatigue can have an impact on your performance."

Air safety boss 'trying to understand' Sydney Airport incident reporting delay A third safety issue on the tarmac at Sydney Airport prompted the nation's air safety boss question why investigators were not notified for four days about another incident on Sunday.

Last week, Minister for Transport Catherine King released a statement after a meeting with the Airservices Australia boss to discuss the airport's challenges.

"It has been a big focus of ours to encourage more people to enter the profession, and 95 people are expected to be endorsed as air traffic controllers by the end of the year," Ms King said.

"Six controllers are currently training in Sydney Tower, with another 15 expected to commence before the end of 2027."

Ms King said the company commitment to improving roster practices for Sydney's air traffic controllers would begin in early September, and that a new Sydney Tower simulator had been installed to increase training capacity.

Mr Sharp said there had been a 44 per cent decrease in delays at the airport over the past two years, and the organisation was focused on the "structural challenge" of the shortage of air traffic controllers.

title: FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs
text:
FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, has left soccer's governing body, weeks after he publicly criticised president Gianni Infantino's plan to sell a stake in its tournament business, including the World Cup.

"FIFA can confirm that the working relationship between FIFA and Kevin Lamour as FIFA's chief operating officer has ended on 17 August 2026," a FIFA spokesperson said.

How Gianni Infantino's FIFA leadership imploded over two weeks The FIFA president has faced more than a fortnight of international turmoil, embroiled in a World Cup sell-off saga that sparked loss of confidence in his leadership.

"FIFA thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter."

Lamour had publicly criticised the proposal last month, saying FIFA staff had been "deceived" over the plan and describing it as "the project of one person".

"Our mission … is to serve football. Not to serve the personal interests of a person who, unfortunately, believes he embodies FIFA when he is supposed to be at its service," Lamour said in a statement at the time.

Lamour's comments came hours after Carlos Cordeiro, a senior adviser to Infantino, resigned in protest at the proposal, calling it "a bad deal for football".

The internal dissent came as FIFA faced widespread opposition to its plan to create a $US20 billion ($28.1 billion) subsidiary to run its tournaments, including the World Cup, and sell up to a 20 per cent stake to external investors. FIFA subsequently abandoned the proposal following the backlash.

title: Australia news LIVE: Labor signs off on gambling reform deal with Coalition; Trump threatens to bomb Oman as US-Iran war agreement expires
text:
Labor has crunched the parliamentary timetable to push through proposed laws on gambling advertising, reducing spending on the NDIS, and forcing tech giants to pay for news.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor appears to have struck a deal with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to support Labor’s NDIS cuts, which save more than $35 billion over four years and angered the disability sector.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during question time last month. Alex Ellinghausen

In exchange, Labor will act more quickly on its pledge to clean up an unintended consequence from its property tax changes causing divorcees or spouses of deceased people to lose grandfathered negative gearing and capital gains concessions. Labor previously argued the change would take months, until Taylor demanded a quicker resolution yesterday.

Labor and the Coalition agreed to condense debate on a gambling crackdown and push the bill to the Senate by tomorrow morning, allowing it to pass the parliament this week.

Labor’s caucus signed off on changes that would create an opt-out register for gambling advertising. Gambling firms will pay for the new register themselves. Inducements to bet will also be cut back. Labor has also shifted from 6am to 5am the start time or a cap of three ads per hour.

Some Coalition MPs want the clampdown on ads to go further. Backbenchers Andrew Wallace, Paul Scarr and Nationals frontbencher Pat Conaghan have all reserved their right to vote against the bill, which Taylor has negotiated with Albanese for a week.

After years of political wrangling, community protests and a failed campaign to preserve one of Sydney’s long-held suburban sporting grounds, residents have been given their clearest picture yet of a proposed transformation of TG Millner Reserve in Marsfield. A $128.9 million plan lodged with Ryde Council this week shows the former spiritual home of Eastwood Rugby Club is one step closer to being bulldozed to make way for a 106-home housing estate. A concept image of the $129 million redevelopment of the site. The proposal marks a major milestone in a bitter battle that has pitted Ryde Council against the NSW government, divided residents and highlighted growing tensions between housing growth and the increasing pressure on sporting fields across Sydney. The plans by TGM Developer Pty Ltd, a consortium involving property developer Winston Langley and the Abadeen Group, represent a significant departure from an earlier proposal for 132 seniors housing dwellings on the site. Instead, the revised plan would deliver 106 private homes ranging from three to five bedrooms.

Advertisement

The six-hectare development would involve the demolition of the district-grade rugby field, grandstand, North Ryde RSL Sports Club and Guardian Childcare Marsfield, a 78-place centre operating within the site. It is understood families were informed in January that the centre would cease operating in December 2026 and families would be supported to transition to alternative nearby services. Development plans lodged with the council describe the project as a “garden neighbourhood” designed to balance housing supply with open space. The proposal includes a new public park and the planting of 456 trees, offsetting the loss of 253 existing trees that would be removed during construction works. The sports ground is a step closer to being transformed into homes. The unveiling of the plans is the latest chapter in the fraught history of the site, which has served as the home of Eastwood Rugby and generations of its members and supporters since 1950. In more recent decades, however, the club has faced increasing financial pressures as participation in local rugby union declined and the club’s players, members and sponsors increasingly shifted towards Sydney’s rapidly growing north-west.

Advertisement

Planning documents to the council stated suburban development around the fields has also created ongoing conflicts over parking, lighting and match-day crowds, limiting opportunities to expand operations. As ageing facilities became increasingly expensive to maintain, Eastwood Rugby and North Ryde RSL – which acquired the site in 2017 – ultimately opted to relocate to a new Centre of Excellence at Fred Caterson Reserve, almost 20 kilometres away in Castle Hill. Ryde Council has consistently opposed any redevelopment of the site. Janie Barrett To help fund the move, TG Millner Reserve was sold to TGM Landowner Pty Ltd in December last year. Ryde Council has consistently opposed residential development of the site, arguing the loss of TG Millner would worsen a shortage of sporting fields as housing development accelerates across surrounding suburbs including Macquarie Park and North Ryde.

Between 2018 and 2020, the council explored heritage listing the site but abandoned the effort after independent studies found it lacked sufficient local heritage significance. It later set aside $15 million and sought state approval to compulsorily acquire the land. However, the bid collapsed when Local Government Minister Ron Hoenig rejected the request, citing concerns about the council’s ability to fund both the purchase and ongoing maintenance of the site. A concept image of the development. The council has continued to campaign against the redevelopment. Last month, Mayor Trenton Brown described TG Millner as critical community infrastructure and launched a $40,000 council-funded campaign urging the community to support efforts to save the fields and pressure Planning Minister Paul Scully to reject the rezoning. But councillor Lyndal Howison, who is Labor’s candidate for Ryde at next year’s state election, warned the campaign risked creating false hope, noting the Sydney North Planning Panel had already determined the proposal had strategic merit and should proceed through the planning system.

In its 2025 ruling, the panel found the redevelopment would help deliver much-needed “missing middle” housing – a decision welcomed by North Ryde RSL chief executive Joe Kelly, who said redevelopment would help secure the long-term future of both the RSL and Eastwood Rugby. Brent edged higher to $US91.15 a barrel after President Donald Trump said he wasn’t interested in extending the expiring agreement with Iran and fighting flared anew in Lebanon. Its price has been careening back and forth because of uncertainty about what the war with Iran will do. Last month alone, Brent zigzagged between $US72 and US102 as hopes rose and fell that the US and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. James Packer James Packer’s bets on AI pay off after sell-down in gaming shares Wall Street has run to records in large part because profits are booming for US companies. Nearly all the companies in the S&P 500 have turned in their profit reports for the Northern hemisphere spring. The average long-term US mortgage rate has already jumped near its highest level in a year because of the rise in the 10-year Treasury yield. title: Women’s physical and mental health 'inseparable', new endometreosis research finds
text:
in brief Almost half of women with endometriosis reported experiencing anxiety.

One in three women experiencing mental health issues are not seeking help.

Women living with endometriosis, ovarian cysts and hormone-related conditions are experiencing significantly higher rates of anxiety, depression and self-harm, highlighting the need for mental health support to be integrated into women’s physical healthcare.

Research published by Women's Mental Health Australia on Tuesday found almost half of women with endometriosis reported experiencing anxiety.

Women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome experienced depression and anxiety at up to twice the rate of women without the condition.

The findings have uncovered major gaps in Australia's healthcare system, according to chief operating officer Katrina Locandro.

"It's enormous," she told the Australian Associated Press.

"The government's investing a lot in women's health at the moment ... and there is a really practical step that they could be taking to reduce that gap."

The findings indicate that physical health conditions are associated with poorer mental health.

But the greatest psychological toll is on women living with female-specific physical health conditions, including polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, a broad condition involving a hormone imbalance, irregular periods and ovarian cysts.

Women with that syndrome reported high rates of depression and anxiety, between 1.6 and 2.2 times higher than women who did not have the condition.

The disparity also extended to suicide and self-harm rates, reported by 10 per cent of women with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome and 13 per cent of women with endometriosis, compared with four per cent of women without those conditions.

The research found that one in three women are not seeking help for their mental health issues, often because of financial and stigma-related reasons.

Locandro says every woman attending a government-funded endometriosis and pelvic pain clinic should receive an integrated mental health assessment and support as a standard offering.

"We're not asking the government to build a new system, we're asking it to strengthen an existing one by recognising that women's physical and mental health are inseparable," she said.

Report co-author Bronwyn Graham said that embedding integrated mental health assessment and support into existing services would be a game-changer.

"Women are being asked to manage two separate journeys, one for their body and one for their mind, and to find their own way between them at the point they are least able to."

title: A high-stakes vote on wealth, power and inequality is looming
text:
In brief California will vote on a proposed wealth tax in November.

Home to many billionaires and their companies, the proposed tax has many supporters — and powerful critics.

In November, California will vote on a proposal to levy a one-off 5 per cent tax on the wealth of all billionaires in the state.

Google co-founder and billionaire Sergey Brin has already spent US$100 million on political donations to a group opposing the tax. Brin is hoping to avoid a potential tax bill of US$13 billion, a return of roughly 130-to-1 if that investment is successful.

Advocates of the billionaire tax claim it would raise US$100 billion in revenue, to be allocated directly to state-funded healthcare, food assistance and public education.

Supporters of the union-backed proposal also highlight that most billionaires currently pay lower marginal rates of tax than the average worker, and that the revenue is desperately needed to fill gaps in funding created by US President Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid.

Its critics, which include California’s Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom, argue the measure will drive billionaires and their tax revenue to leave the state.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Taxing the ultrawealthy

Similar measures targeting the ultrawealthy are currently under consideration around the world.

In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has proposed a 2 per cent income tax increase for those earning over US$1 million, and passed a property surcharge tax on second homes. Other US states — including Washington state, Maine and Minnesota — have passed or are considering similar income or wealth tax measures.

In the United Kingdom, a group of 120 millionaires have launched a “Proud to Pay” campaign asking the government to levy an additional 2% tax on wealth over £10 million.

Spiralling global inequality

Behind the public discussion of California’s billionaire tax lies a much deeper debate about spiralling global inequality.

Recent data from the US shows the share of economic output flowing to workers has dropped to a record low of 52.9 per cent in 2026. This means for every US$100 the economy produces, workers take home US$52.90 in pay, the smallest share since records began in 1947.

Similar trends have been observed around the world.

READ MORE Musk becomes first trillionaire in history as SpaceX shares soar

Conversely, the wealth of billionaires has accelerated rapidly. As of 2026, Forbes reports a global record 3,428 billionaires.

Perhaps most symptomatically, in June Elon Musk briefly became the world’s first trillionaire after the public launch of SpaceX. His wealth now sits at around US$800 billion.

The causes of inequality

Some blame globalisation for this explosion of inequality, but there are two other important related factors to consider as well.

The first is the global decline of the trade union movement. With union membership and power declining around the world, the ability of workers to negotiate for better wages has declined.

The second is a trend of corporate consolidation into a small number of large superstar firms. These companies, which include tech giants like Alphabet, Amazon, and Uber, wield monopoly-like powers. This reduces competition and allows these firms to drive down wages.

The rise of artificial intelligence and automation will only accelerate these trends, enabling the largest firms to shed even more workers even as the firms’ output and profitability continues to climb.

Workers feel the crunch

For the last couple of decades, stagnating wages have been propped up by cheap access to credit. With central banks using unconventional policies to keep interest rates low, household spending has remained largely stable, funded by an increase in household debt.

However, with inflation rising, central banks around the world have pushed up interest rates from emergency lows during the pandemic, cutting off the source of cheap credit. With inflation rising faster than wages, the effect has been real declines in living standards.

Unsurprisingly, voters are unhappy at this “cost of living” crisis, and all over the world have turned away from incumbents and established parties.

A jump to the left?

If the previous decade’s politics have been dominated by dissent on the right, many countries are now seeing the emergence of stronger dissent on the left.

After Mamdani’s headline-grabbing victory in New York, Democratic Socialists have ridden a wave of momentum to win a series of primary races. Beyond the US, we can note left-independent Catherine Connolly’s election as Irish president, the rise of the Greens in the UK, and the recent resurgence of left-wing Die Linke in Germany.

These different parties and leaders all share a focus on combating growing global inequalities of wealth and power. Billionaires, the most obvious and visible symbol of global wealth inequalities, are an obvious target.

However, as California’s proposal shows, attempts to rein in the wealth and power of billionaires should expect furious backlash from billionaires themselves.

In addition to Brin’s US$100 million, other billionaire donors including Peter Thiel, Eric Schmidt and Chris Larsen have also spent significantly to oppose the tax. Brin’s campaign committee has also organised competing ballot propositions which, if passed, would nullify the tax.

For now, polling suggests the billionaire tax is supported by a majority of voters. More than 1.6 million Californians signed the petition to put the tax on the November ballot.

The future of wealth inequality

California’s coming election will serve as an important test of the political power of the billionaire class, and the broader health of American democracy.

Yet even if the tax is successful, taxing billionaires only treats a symptom of global inequality, rather than addressing its underlying causes.

A policy agenda for seriously addressing wealth inequality must also therefore include a much broader suite of measures. These might include improving workers’ bargaining power, breaking up monopolies and public ownership of AI technology.

Without these structural fixes, we should expect voter anger and the current political instability around the world to continue to escalate.

title: The costly contradiction hiding in Australian kitchens
text:
In brief Australians are resorting to eating expired food to save money, according to a new survey.

At the same time, more than 7 million tonnes of food is wasted in Australia each year, amid confusion over what's actually expired and what isn't.

As Australians look for ways to cut grocery costs, confusing food date labels could be driving people to throw out food that's still perfectly safe to eat.

New survey data from financial comparison site Finder suggests 14 per cent of Australians say they've resorted to eating expired food to save money, while 68 per cent of the 1,010 survey participants said they've taken money-saving measures to afford food.

At the same time, confusion over what "use-by" and "best-before" dates actually mean could be costing households at the other end.

OzHarvest has been campaigning for reforms to Australia's date label system, arguing that "evidence has moved on" since it was established more than two decades ago.

The food rescue organisation says date labelling is a major driver of unnecessary food waste.

Research commissioned by the group found food reaching its best-before or use-by date was the most commonly cited reason for disposal, reported by 58 per cent of high-wasting households and 44 per cent of low-waste households.

"Consumers are really confused by the difference between best-before and use-by," said RMIT associate professor Lukas Parker, who has authored research on the topic with End Food Waste Australia.

"We know it's around 50 per cent or more of people just don't know the difference," he told SBS News.

A 2021 government-backed national study estimated Australian households throw away up to $2,500 worth of food each year, with 7.6 million tonnes of food wasted annually — around 300kg per person.

When is food actually expired?

The term "use-by" means the food carrying the label can only be guaranteed safe to consume until that date. Highly perishable products like fresh meat might carry this label.

A "best-before" date, on the other hand, means the product is still safe to consume after that date, but it might no longer be at its best. Products like cereals and pasta might come with a "best-before" label.

Food suppliers are responsible for putting these dates on their products.

According to Food Standards Australia New Zealand, you can still eat foods for a while after the best-before date. They may have lost some quality, but they can still be sold and consumed after the best-before date has passed.

Foods cannot legally be sold after the use-by date, the food standards regulator says.

But many consumers treat both dates the same, according to OzHarvest, meaning food that's safe to eat ends up in the bin.

The 'sniff' test?

OzHarvest says people should trust their instincts and senses when deciding whether food past its date needs to go in the bin or is still safe to eat.

"Sniff a product, look at a product, taste it to see if it is okay," its national policy and advocacy lead Katinka Day says.

"We're really supportive of additional information on packets next to that best-before label that encourages people to think, to sniff, look, taste."

The organisation is also advocating for certain products, including milk, to be moved from "use-by" labelling to "best-before", encouraging consumers to use their senses to assess whether a product is safe to consume.

In the UK, some major supermarkets have replaced use-by dates with best-before dates on milk in a bid to reduce the hundreds of thousands of tonnes of milk wasted each year. Consumers are instead encouraged to use a sniff test to determine whether it has spoiled.

Food safety experts agreed that sensory cues can be useful for foods past their best-before date, but warned the "sniff test" shouldn't be treated as a blanket rule for determining whether any food is safe to eat.

Food Safety Information Council CEO Lydia Buchtmann warned that relying on a smell alone for certain products can be dangerous, telling SBS News that food can smell completely normal and still contain disease-causing bacteria or viruses.

Julian Cox, an associate professor of food microbiology at the University of New South Wales, said the level of risk depends on the type of food.

For example, he told SBS News canned foods and shelf-stable products like cereals that have passed their best-before date are generally safe to assess via a smell test.

For more perishable foods, however, the picture is more complicated. While it's easy to detect if an orange has gone mouldy, he said, a piece of cut rockmelon is a "beautiful growth medium for bad bugs" that might still look and smell normal.

For items like meat, he said, a use-by date means exactly that.

Preventing food waste — and saving money

Clearer date labelling could help consumers keep food for longer, reducing both household costs and the environmental impact of food waste.

Parker said his research initiative has been working to reimagine the way labels are presented to consumers.

"[We are] looking at ways to help avoid the confusion of the dates, but also providing consumers really helpful ways to extend the life of their food," he said.

Some brands have already started implementing changes, including Nestlé, which has introduced a label on some of its MAGGI instant noodles products that reads: "If past the date, sniff, look or taste to avoid food waste".

Parker said: "Something like instant noodles, for instance, is going to last a very long time, and they're really well kept inside plastic and very stable."

Some MAGGI 2-minute noodles products now carry a "Sniff, Look, Taste" logo. Credit: Nestlé

"So the best-before is really just a date that people should be using as a means to rotate the food in their house, rather than actually something that would you would use to throw out food."

Cox said consumers can extend the shelf life of food with a best-before date by paying attention to storage conditions and whether the packaging has been opened.

"The idea of the cool, dark place for even quite shelf-stable foods is really important," he said.

title: The surprising backstory behind a popular cold 'remedy'
text:
In brief There's limited evidence that vitamin C is beneficial for a cold.

A Nobel Prize winner's book is widely credited with sparking the belief.

From the first hint of cold winter mornings, supermarkets and pharmacies begin heavy marketing to coax us to stock up on vitamin C to get through the cold and flu season.

But where did that idea come from?

As we'll see, it’s a story including a Nobel Prize winner, a book and some claims that don’t quite stack up.

Nobel Prize winner writes a book

Linus Pauling was a chemist from the United States who won two Nobel Prizes. One was in 1954 for chemistry, for his research into chemical bonds. The other was in 1962 for peace, for his activism against nuclear weapons testing.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

He was not a dietitian or an infectious disease physician. But that didn’t stop him publishing a book on vitamin C and colds in 1970. This book is widely credited with the skyrocketing sales of vitamin C at the time, a trend that continues today.

In this book, Pauling said we should consume high doses of vitamin C, around 1,000–2,000 milligrams a day for good health, and even more to prevent a cold.

READ MORE The three winter bugs facing Australians — and how to tell which you have

His recommendations were said to be initially from one placebo-controlled trial in children on a ski camp in the Swiss Alps. He then analysed a further four studies conducted after his claims.

But his interpretation of these studies has been widely criticised. There were incorrect mathematical analyses, reliance on four poor-quality trials and the overemphasis of the study in children.

So, do mega-doses of vitamin C work?

The short answer is not really. Multiple studies conducted since the ones Pauling analysed show that if there is an effect on vitamin C and colds, it’s minimal. Even then, any marginal benefits are only under certain circumstances, such as if you’re an athlete or in the army.

One study, published in 2023, was a meta-analysis that combined the results of ten placebo-controlled trials. These looked at the effect of vitamin C on the severity and duration of colds. In total, these trials involved 2,736 healthy people (adults, children and athletes) who regularly took at least 1,000mg of vitamin C a day, not just when they had a cold.

Overall, the researchers found people who took vitamin C had a 15 per cent reduction in severe cold symptoms compared to those who didn’t take it. This was expressed as the number of days "confined indoors", which the authors acknowledged as a limitation. Vitamin C did not affect how long mild symptoms lasted.

READ MORE Feeling congested this winter? A common medicinal ingredient might not be helping

A meta-analysis in 2013 found taking lower doses (at around 200mg a day) did not decrease the number of colds in the general population. However, there were fewer colds for athletes and army personnel.

Similar to the other study, regular vitamin C supplements showed a reduction in severity of symptoms in children and adults by 8–14 per cent. However, taking vitamin C at the start of the cold had no benefit.

So, from these two meta-analyses, Pauling’s original advice is over-stated. There is no evidence vitamin C will reduce your risk of catching a cold.

READ MORE Researchers discover new clue that helps explain severe COVID-19

There is some evidence it will reduce how long severe symptoms last, but on average only by about 10 per cent. So if severe symptoms from a cold last for five days, it will reduce severe symptoms by about 12 hours. If the severe symptoms last for 24 hours, they will reduce by about two-and-a-half hours.

Taking vitamin C when symptoms start will have no effect. You need to be taking it regularly, even before you get sick.

So how much vitamin C is too much?

Pauling’s recommendation for good health, at around 1,000–2,000mg a day, is around the upper limit of what’s now considered safe to consume.

Australia has not set an upper limit for vitamin C, due to inconclusive evidence. But guidelines refer to other expert recommendations for adults to not consume more than 1,000mg a day. In the United States, the upper limit for adults is 2,000mg a day.

Pauling’s recommendation is also much higher than the recommended daily intake in Australia and other countries. For adults over 19 in Australia, this is 45mg.

This is what you would find in half an orange, three to four florets of cooked broccoli or one-third of a glass of orange juice.

So what should I do?

Taking high doses of vitamin C (over 1,000mg a day) continually can increase your risk of adverse events such as:

Gastrointestinal effects, such as diarrhoea, nausea, stomach cramps and bloating

More oxalate excretion, which may lead to kidney stones

An increase in iron absorption, which may lead to tissue damage in people with undiagnosed haemochromatosis (an inherited disorder where you absorb too much iron from your food)

Interactions with radiation therapy, chemotherapy and the cholesterol-lowering drugs statins.

If you feel you would benefit from vitamin C supplements, discuss this with your GP. You should limit the dose to below 1,000mg a day and be mindful of the side effects.

Remember less than 4 per cent of Australians are deficient in vitamin C.

Evangeline Mantzioris is the program director of human nutrition at Adelaide University and an accredited practising dietitian. title: Government unveils last-minute gambling reforms ahead of critical new report
text:
Sweeping last-minute changes to Labor's gambling reforms, including a crackdown on inducements, have been unveiled in parliament, hours before the release of a damning report on the matter.

A Senate committee report on the proposed changes was tabled on Monday night, slamming the government's attempt to protect vulnerable people from gambling addictions as being too little, too late.

It contained criticism from the coalition, Greens and independent senator David Pocock.

The reforms were referred to the committee for an inquiry over concerns they did not adequately break the connection between betting and sport nor protect kids from gambling exposure.

"This package is not an evidence-led public health response to a public health issue," Pocock said in the report.
