Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It leaves gambling advertising embedded in sport and across Australian media, shifts responsibility onto parents and preserves major parts of the system that have made Australians the biggest gambling losers in the world on a per capita basis."

But the government appeared to anticipate the report's critical contents.

Amendments to the reforms, announced just hours before the report was tabled, included restrictions on inducements and limited commissions for affiliate agents

The changes respond to concerns from the Greens, who said they would not support the bill in its earlier form.

"Inducements are a toxic practice that prey on those who can least afford to gamble and must be outlawed," Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said.

"Gambling companies must not be allowed to continue to make massive profits off vulnerable people."

The government also pledged a new opt-out register for gambling ads, which would allow Australians to sign up for a one-stop shop for removing the ads from online platforms.

It would function similarly to the Do Not Call register for spam calls, following concerns raised that people would struggle to stay on top of individual opt-out options on each online service.

A levy would be imposed on gambling companies to cover the cost of the register, Communications Minister Anika Wells told parliament.

But critics of the government's work, including the coalition, have said the drawn-out changes were far too delayed.

A report by late Labor MP Peta Murphy into the matter was published in 2023 and contained more than 30 recommendations to limit the power of Australia's gambling industry.

Feedback in the committee report noted many of the recommendations had not been included in the reforms.

"Even the government's response to this (Murphy's) report, tabled on May 12, 2026 — the day of the federal budget when many journalists were in the budget lock-up — became a cynical exercise in media management," the coalition said in its response.

The amendments are expected to be debated on Tuesday and signify an end to lengthy pushback from the coalition and crossbench.

Reforms are likely to proceed quickly through both houses by the end of the sitting week, though the coalition has not yet publicly committed to supporting the package.

title: When should you be able to access your super? Battle lines are being drawn
text:
in brief Labor says it will defend Australia's superannuation scheme after criticism from the Coalition and One Nation.

Liberal senator Andrew Bragg said the scheme was "illiberal", while One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said it was "broken".

Political battle lines are being drawn over superannuation, with Labor vowing to defend the retirement savings system as the Liberal Party and One Nation attack it as a failure.

On Monday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers signalled super could become a political issue at the next federal election.

"The stakes are high at the next election for a whole range of reasons, and one of them now is the future of Australia's world-leading compulsory superannuation system," Chalmers told reporters as he arrived at Parliament House.

"The Liberals, the Nationals, and One Nation would end compulsory superannuation as we know it. Their policy and their ideology on super would absolutely decimate the economic security and retirement incomes of millions of Australian workers.

"They share a dangerous and divisive anti-worker, anti-super ideology, and if this plays out after the next election, Australian workers will be much worse off."

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

However a senior Liberal senator later sought to dispute that was the party's ambition.

The stoush began last week when Liberal senator Andrew Bragg declared superannuation an "illiberal experiment".

READ MORE There's another reason to check who inherits your superannuation

"It’s one of the biggest public policy failures since federation, in the sense that it hasn’t helped the budget, and it has not really helped many people get off the pension," he told ABC radio on Thursday.

"What it has done is it has created a huge viper's nest for banks and financiers and unions to pilfer, which is why what you saw at the Labor Party conference was now you're going to have super for under 18s."

The Association of Superannuation Funds Australia (ASFA) refuted Bragg's comments, pointing out Australia's age pension expenditure had decreased since the scheme was introduced in 1992.

"Super has meant that even as our population ages, the government's Age Pension bill is going down instead of up. OECD projections have Australia at the lowest public pension spending in the OECD by the mid-2030s," ASFA CEO Mary Delahunty said.

"Super has also meant that reliance on the Age Pension has fallen, with 12 per cent fewer over-65s receiving a part or full Age Pension today than in 2012. This will keep falling as we see the effects of higher super guarantees coming in.

"A lower reliance on the Age Pension is a massive public policy success."

Under the current system, all Australian employers are required to pay a minimum 12 per cent of an employee's salary into a nominated super fund, which cannot be accessed until a person is 60.

Chalmers 'making things up': Hume

Deputy Opposition leader Jane Hume said the Liberals would not make any changes to compulsory super, saying the treasurer was "simply making things up".

"I think the treasurer has taken a leaf out of the Mad Men Don Draper book; if you don’t like what they’re saying about you, change the conversation. Can I make it very clear: the super guarantee is here to stay," she told reporters in Canberra.

Hume said the Coalition would consider adopting an early super access policy, telling News24 economic security in retirement hinged on home ownership, rather than a person's superannuation balance.

The Coalition has taken a "super for housing" policy to the last two elections, which would allow first-home buyers to withdraw up to $50,000 to buy a property.

On Sunday, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson waded into the debate, labelling Australia's superannuation scheme "broken" and suggesting financially struggling Australians should be able to access super early.

"A lot of Australians are doing it tough now and struggling to pay off their mortgages," she told News24 on Sunday, adding the policy proposal was yet to be finalised.

"In some ways, I feel that you should give them their money now, and let them help them with the cost of living."

Hanson's deputy, Barnaby Joyce, backed those calls, telling Seven that the current rules only allowed early access in extremely limited circumstances, such as medical treatment.

"I think one of the hardships people have is if they can't feed themselves. And another hardship is if they don't have a house and they're put out on the street and they're living in a car," he said on Monday.

"Surely it's their money and we should give a little more respect about what they can do with their own money."

Labor's assistant minister for housing, Julian Hill, said accessing super early to pay for housing deserves "a gold medal for the stupidest policy".

title: Pauline Hanson still doesn't like Mardi Gras, says sexuality should be 'behind closed doors'
text:
In brief Pauline Hanson says she doesn't intend to go to Mardi Gras and believes people should keep their sexuality "behind closed doors".

The senator has also defended her inability to name the leaders of crucial regional powers.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has doubled down on notorious decades-old comments criticising Sydney's Mardi Gras, saying she thinks people should keep their sexuality "behind closed doors".

The comments come only days after a colleague declared One Nation "one of the gayest parties in Australia".

In an infamous 1996 interview with 60 Minutes, Hanson responded "I don't like it" while offering her thoughts on the annual LGBTQI+ festival.

"I don't like it because it's promoting something ... that is not natural," she said at the time.

Her "I don't like it" comment was co-opted by musician Simon Hunt, also known as drag queen Pauline Pantsdown, in 1998, and remixed into a parody dance song that made the Triple J Hottest 100 that year.

Musician Simon Hunt, also known as drag queen Pauline Pantsdown, had a hit dance song parodying Pauline Hanson. Source: AAP / Danny Casey

Three decades later, Hanson said she acknowledged the economic benefit of the pride parade, adding that it was "acceptable" Australia had legalised gay marriage.

"I still don't like the gay Mardi Gras, but that's my opinion," she told News24 on Sunday.

"Have I ever been to one? No. Do I intend to go? No, I don't.

"I think your own personal sexuality should be kept ... behind closed doors. It's no one's business to do it out there with the gay Mardi Gras anywhere.

"I know it brings a lot of tourists to the country. I know it brings a lot of money. I know all this, but that’s my personal opinion. But anyway, good luck to them that they want to do that."

Her comments follow revelations One Nation's candidate for Western Australia's upper house at the 2025 election, Parminder Singh, made several anti-gay comments in a video on social media.

Singh, who was third on One Nation's upper house ticket at the state election, has since been removed from the party's website.

During the week, One Nation MP Barnaby distanced the party from its former candidate's views, describing it as "one of the gayest parties in Australia".

Hanson also rejected Singh's comments, saying she never heard similar views from him when he was a candidate.

"That's his personal thoughts and not my thoughts whatsoever," she said.

Hanson defends inability to name world leaders

The firebrand politician also defended her inability to name the leaders of crucial allies and regional powers when questioned about her foreign policy credentials as a would-be prime minister.

In an earlier interview with News24, the One Nation leader said diplomacy with Australia's neighbours would pose "no problem", despite her notoriously using her maiden speech in 1996 to declare the nation was "in danger of being swamped by Asians".

Asked if she could name the president of Indonesia or the prime minister of Japan, two major regional powers and key Australian trading partners, Hanson said she couldn't.

On Sunday, she said she would learn the names when it was necessary.

"I still haven't looked up who the prime minister of Indonesia is because I don't need to know ... I'm not the foreign minister, I'm not the prime minister," Hanson said.

The One Nation leader also reiterated her party's position that Australia's net migration target should be 130,000 a year — a significant cut on current levels.

She suggested the reduction could come at the expense of international students, a major source of income for universities, describing the intake system as a "farce" and a "scam" that provides a backdoor into the nation.

But she was adamant any cut to migration should not alter backpacker levels.

"We cannot stop those people coming in; if they did, the farmers would go under," Hanson said.

None of the major parties have outlined which visa categories should be cut to meet their reduced migration targets.

title: Fiji, Israel and the Lost Tribe at the ends of the Earth
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Long ago, the story goes, a great double-hulled canoe called the Kaunitoni came from the west, carrying the first ancestral chiefs of the iTaukei (indigenous Fijians). At its head, in one version of the tradition, stood their leader, Lutunasobasoba.

The voyagers had come a seemingly impossible distance: from Thebes in ancient Egypt — earlier still, some say, from a place farther west, via Israel — down the Nile to Lake Tanganyika, across the Indian Ocean, and finally to Vuda, on the western coast of Viti Levu, Fiji's largest island.

Somewhere in that crossing, a sacred box went over the side.

In some tellings, it carried the written record of the people's laws and genealogies — lost, like the canoe's other cargo, somewhere in the churning sea.

For most of the past century, this has been one of the best-known versions of Fiji's national origin story. The mission schools taught it; so did the primary schools. Radio carried it further still, until it became part of the way generations of Fijians understood their ancestry.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Only, much of it was invented in the 1890s — set down for the first time in a newspaper.

The colonial government's Fijian-language paper, Na Mata, ran a competition at the time, inviting readers across the archipelago to send in the definitive account of where the Fijian people had come from, with the best to be printed.

The winning entry ran over 17 instalments, centring on a forgotten tribe. Within a few decades it had acquired the weight of history.

The shape of the belief

The story of the Kaunitoni is only one part of the overall narrative.

Behind the claimed migration sits a larger conviction, still widely held in some iTaukei communities and church groups: that Fijians descend from a Lost Tribe of Israel — one of 10 the Hebrew Bible describes as carried into exile and never heard from again.

The belief has no support in mainstream science or archaeology. Yet it has helped foster a distinctive affinity with Israel.

An artistic depiction of the Kaunitoni, the double-hulled canoe at the centre of Fiji's best-known origin story. Source: SBS News / Jacob Chantarat

The particulars shift from place to place. On Mana Island, in the Yasawa group off western Viti Levu, the Ark of the Covenant — the gold-covered chest that, in the Book of Exodus, held the Ten Commandments — is said to lie buried.

In a village in Ba, in Viti Levu's north-west, an elder once pointed to a rock and told Reverend Marika Baleidelabaci, a Fijian historian and Methodist minister, that Jesus had been born exactly there.

In the Navosa highlands, markings cut into a cave wall are read by some as ancient Hebrew — an interpretation, Baleidelabaci says, that came back with Fijian soldiers who had served in the Middle East and recognised the shapes.

"Nobody knows the origin of that writing," he tells SBS News of the unverified petroglyphs.

They assumed that it must be Jewish.

Believers offer corroborations: circumcision is said to predate the missionaries; Fiji is read as an acronym for Father of Israel, Jewish Island; the tanoa, the carved bowl in which the yaqona (kava) drink is served, is claimed to take its name from a phrase meaning "built by Noah".

Anthropologist Lynda Newland, writing in 2015, described the idea that certain iTaukei clans descend from a Lost Tribe as "very strong among some contemporary clans and church groups". Her research traces the belief through the intersection of Christianity, Fijian traditions and ideas about ancestry.

Edwin Jones, who spent a year in the highland district of Nabobuco, found it had "gained currency" among Methodists of the interior — held there alongside their own belief that the ancestors emerged from the Nakauvadra hills.

Christians make up around two-thirds of Fiji's population, and more than half of them are Methodist — a church whose preaching draws heavily on the Hebrew Bible. One former president of the Methodist Church in Fiji estimated 95 per cent of sermons were taken from the Old Testament.

A map of the Kaunitoni voyage as the story describes it — out of Egypt, along the African lakes, and east across two oceans. Source: SBS News

Beyond Fiji, iterations of the same idea have taken root across Melanesia.

In western Papua New Guinea, the Gogodala have been reported to perform Hebrew prayers and incorporate biblical-Israelite ideas into religious practice.

On Malaita, the most populous island of Solomon Islands, the late Anglican visionary George Umai taught that his ancestors had fled Jerusalem in the first century and buried the Ark in the bush at Kwara'ae. There, Israeli flags still hang in village churches, a visible expression of the close ties some Pacific communities have developed with their perceived motherland.

Why the Pacific votes with Israel

In the past three years, that connection has become visible in foreign policy.

When the United Nations General Assembly voted in October 2023 on a ceasefire in Gaza, 14 countries opposed it. Six were Pacific Island states: Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Nauru, Tonga, the Marshall Islands and Micronesia — among the smallest nations on Earth and together accounting for nearly half of the votes against the resolution.

The resolution called for an immediate humanitarian truce but did not explicitly mention Hamas' October 7 attacks, an omission several countries, including Fiji, cited in explaining their objections.

Fijian Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka (left) and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the opening of Fiji's embassy in Jerusalem on 17 September 2025. Credit: Fiji Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Fiji's position is also shaped by domestic politics.

The country's Jerusalem embassy, opened in September 2025, has its roots in a 2022 election that left parliament deadlocked and gave the nationalist Social Democratic Liberal Party (SODELPA) the balance of power in coalition talks. SODELPA leader Viliame Gavoka had campaigned on a promise to establish an embassy in Jerusalem. Sitiveni Rabuka, who became prime minister after forming a coalition with SODELPA, agreed to the proposal, with Gavoka becoming his deputy.

Meanwhile, Papua New Guinea opened an embassy in Jerusalem in 2023, with Israel underwriting the running costs. Samoa announced its own in early 2026, and in July, Nauru became the latest Pacific country to announce plans to do so.

Jerusalem's status remains sensitive and complex, as it is contested between the Israelis and the Palestinians. The Israelis claim it as their capital, and Israel's parliament, the Knesset, is based there.

For Palestinians, it is their historical, religious and cultural capital, home to the Al-Aqsa Mosque, considered the third holiest site in Islam, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the most sacred site in Christianity.

Israel has occupied East Jerusalem since 1967, annexing the area in 1980.

Fiji has contributed troops to UN peacekeeping missions in the Middle East since the late 1970s, and remains among the largest per-capita contributors of peacekeepers in the world. Source: AP / Hanin Network Website

Israel has been expanding in the other direction too, opening an embassy in Fiji's capital Suva in June — a regional hub intended to deepen ties with Fiji and across the wider Pacific.

But the political relationship has another layer. Behind the growth in political ties is decades of work by the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (ICEJ), an evangelical Christian Zionist group founded in 1980 that has campaigned in Pacific churches for years, and whose Fiji branch its leadership has praised as a model for pro-Israel Christians worldwide. SBS News contacted the ICEJ for comment but received no response.

The attachment to the holy land is expressed in other ways too. Relative to its population, Fiji has sent more soldiers to UN peacekeeping missions than any other country in the world — many of which have been carried out in the Middle East. Believers of the Kaunitoni origin story also make regular pilgrimages to Israel.

In early October 2023, Fijian pilgrims stood in the Negev desert near the Gaza border, planting oak seedlings in the dry yellow dirt and watering them from a bottle of Fiji Water. They had travelled for Sukkot, the Jewish harvest festival, believing themselves to be returning to ancestral land.

Two days later, Hamas militants led the coordinated October 7 attack into southern Israel, leading to Israel's invasion of the now-devastated enclave.

Brian Dunn is a church historian who emigrated to Fiji from Canada in mid-2023 and is now the head of history at Pasifika Communities University. He says many of those who have returned from peacekeeping tours describe them in unexpectedly personal terms.

"Some even looked at their tour of duty as a pilgrimage," Dunn tells SBS News.

"I hadn't really noticed until October 7 just how fully and completely it seems like the vast majority of Fijians were putting their support behind the nation state of Israel."

How Fiji's Kaunitoni origin story came to be

To understand how a newspaper entry came to shape Fiji's origin story, we have to go back 40 years before it ran — to two Wesleyan missionaries, William Cross and David Cargill, who landed in 1835 on the island of Lakeba, in Fiji's far east, carrying the Old Testament.

Fijians heard of a people chosen by God and organised into 12 tribes, each descended from a common ancestor — and Fijian society was built the same way, in clans tracing descent from a founding ancestor, each with its own plant or animal totem.

"They tried to assimilate themselves with the Jews," Baleidelabaci says.

The idea took written form in the mission schools. In a 2003 doctoral thesis, the Fijian Methodist minister Tevita Baleiwaqa traces it to the seminary that trained Fiji's first indigenous ministers, where students schooled in the Old Testament began reading their own past through biblical narratives.

Anthropologist Lynda Newland finds no trace of the Lost Tribes idea in Fiji before Cession in 1874 — when sovereignty was handed to Britain — and argues it surfaces a decade or two later — once Christianity and Victorian science had supplied "a grammar for it".

The Israeli and Fijian flags fly outside Suva's Grand Pacific Hotel in late October 2025, weeks after Fiji opened its embassy in Jerusalem. Source: SBS, Supplied

That science was diffusionism: the belief that complex cultural practices could not have developed independently in different places, and must instead have spread from a common ancient source, often located somewhere in the biblical world.

Its method was wordplay. The missionary Jesse Carey, working under the amateur anthropologist Lorimer Fison, gathered resemblances between Fijian and African place names — among them a Vunda near Lake Tanganyika as well as the Vunda in Fiji — and concluded Fijians had come from Africa, and before that from Egypt.

"He homologised these names, though they have no relation whatsoever," Dunn says.

The colonial administration had its own reason to want a single origin story. Fiji had never been one country, but a patchwork of chiefdoms with no paramount ruler — and Britain preferred to govern indirectly, through an existing hierarchy.

A shared ancestry was easier for colonial administrators to govern than a society of hundreds of clans.

READ MORE Former Fiji military commander Sitiveni Rabuka rules out China security pact if he wins government

Which brings the story back to the newspaper. In 1892 the editor of Na Mata announced a competition to select a definitive version of the people's legendary history. No criteria for judging were ever published.

The winning entry ran in seventeen monthly instalments, and its author signed himself Denicagilaba — or Hurricane Clouds.

Three years later Basil Thomson, a colonial official who would go on to chair the Native Lands Commission — the body that decided which clan owned what — translated the story and published it in London.

The identity behind the pseudonym went unrecorded for 70 years. When the historian Peter France established it, on Thomson's authority, Hurricane Clouds turned out to be Ilai Motonococoka — Thomson's own clerk.

"It was like fan fiction," Dunn says.

The ultimate agenda was to bring the land resources under control.

That interpretation is contested, but the story was produced at a time when the colonial government was formalising systems of land ownership and political authority.

Then the empire added a layer. Fiji was expected to pay for itself, and sugar was the crop to do it — but iTaukei land could not be sold, and iTaukei labour could not be easily commandeered for the plantations. So, Britain shipped in workers instead: more than 60,000 Indian indentured labourers arrived between 1879 and 1916, under contracts known as girmit.

To explain two peoples in one colony, missionaries turned to the story of twin brothers Jacob and Esau from the book of Genesis, casting Indo-Fijians as the younger brother Jacob and the iTaukei as Esau the hunter. In the story, the brothers share a lifelong rivalry that culminates in Jacob deceiving his father to gain a blessing intended for his older brother. Missionaries leant on the tale to share a hidden message: the older shall serve the younger.

The 1987 Fiji coups and the politics of identity

In April 1987, an election ended 17 years of rule by the iTaukei-led Alliance Party.

The winning coalition drew its support largely from Indo-Fijians, who by then made up roughly half the population; its prime minister, Timoci Bavadra, was an iTaukei commoner, but most of his cabinet was not.

Within a month, Lieutenant Colonel Sitiveni Rabuka — a Methodist lay preacher — walked into parliament with 10 masked soldiers and removed the government at gunpoint. When a negotiated settlement threatened to restore it in September, he seized power a second time and declared Fiji a republic.

Inside the Methodist Church, the country's largest denomination, a parallel struggle over the church's direction was under way.

For two decades its presidents had been moderates who preached ecumenism (unity among Christian denominations) and multiracialism; the church had elected an Indo-Fijian president as recently as 1977. Manasa Lasaro, its general secretary, moved against that tradition.

Baleidelabaci, who was in Fiji during those years, remembers the language exactly.

"He said the coup was the will of God to free the Fijians, the chosen people, from bondage and from heathen races," he recalls.

"That refers to the Indians."

Lasaro declared Fiji a holy land and its people a holy people, who demanded holy government for all. From the pulpit, Rabuka's soldiers became Joshua, the general who seized Canaan, and the ministers Moses, who brought the people out of bondage.

"The Fijians at that time were only fighting for the rights of the iTaukei," Baleidelabaci says.

"The dominance of iTaukei in Fiji."

Underneath the scripture was a narrative the empire had helped build: one assembled to make Fiji legible to its administrators that had, a century later, been taken up by a nationalist movement — and turned against a population the same empire had brought to the colony.

The Fijian histories left out of the archive

When Dunn repeated the Kaunitoni story to elders in the highland village of Rewasau, deep in the interior and far from the coastal centres where the mission first took hold, they brushed it aside.

"That's not our story," they told him.

We didn't come from anywhere. We've always been here.

Archaeological evidence points to human settlement around 3,000 years ago, associated with the Lapita people, whose distinctive pottery has been found across the Pacific — a very different account from the Kaunitoni story of migration from ancient Egypt.

Baleidelabaci, a Methodist minister himself, is collecting what the archive left out — accounts that survived in the far-flung villages, and nowhere else.

"When they arrived, they said that our stories of our origin were regarded as myths and legends," he says.

"There's a lot of things in my church that need to be reinvestigated. What we are doing now is still new to us."

For Dunn, the correction has to come from the same place the stories do.

"The voice of the communities has really unsettled the text. Most of what actually happened never got written," he says.

Just a tiny sliver made it into the archive — and the very act of writing it into an archive is a power move.

title: 'Won't be the case forever': Australia's housing market is testing a popular assumption
text:
In brief Investors appear to be pulling back but it may be an early reaction to the tax reforms announced in May.

A retreat of investors doesn't mean first-home buyers will fill the gap.

Investors are shying away from the housing market — but experts say it might not be the win the government says it is.

New Australian Bureau of Statistics data on loans show investors have pulled back sharply from the housing market in the June quarter.

Declines in investor loans was the highest since September 2022.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said on Friday the lending figures were an "encouraging sign" that Labor's changes to negative gearing and the capital gains discount were working as intended and the market was "shifting in favour of first-home buyers" — even before the changes have officially taken effect.

But experts said the retreat hasn't necessarily translated into the wave of first-home buyers the federal government's property tax changes were designed to generate.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

'Not surprising' but not the whole picture

The number of investor loans fell 8.6 per cent in the June quarter, while first-home buyer loans fell a comparatively lower 2.9 per cent, according to ABS data released on Friday.

Independent property researcher Cameron Kusher said ABS' latest lending data was not surprising and reflected a typical knee-jerk reaction to policy changes.

“Across both the number and the value, the biggest falls in lending over the quarter were for investors, which is not really a surprise when you consider the tax changes that have happened,” he said.

Both investors and owner-occupiers have shied off the housing market — but investors saw a much larger dip. Source: SBS News

The pullback lines up with what major banks have been reporting in their own lending figures, with CBA and NAB both reporting a 15 per cent drop in mortgage applications last quarter, while Westpac saw a 20 per cent drop.

The tax changes were announced in the May budget but aren't set to formally take effect until 1 July 2027. So, this quarter's fall was a reaction to the announcement itself, not the policy in action.

Kusher expects a bigger fall in investor lending in the future.

"We may actually see a larger fall when we get to the next quarter, when we see the full impact of a whole quarter of these changes," he said.

Both Kusher and Real Estate Group's economist Luc Redman say investors have not retreated entirely, rather they have changed strategy.

They are still keen on residential property but the type of property they’re chasing has shifted. They are now eyeing properties that have strong rental growth, or yield.

"Early evidence post-budget suggests that investors are enquiring more towards units that tend to have a higher yield and a lower entry point … compared to prior, when investors would be looking at houses that have stronger prospects of capital growth," Redman told SBS News.

Two places, Tasmania and the ACT, didn't see drops in investor interest — which Kusher said could be a sign they're moving toward properties with good rental returns relative to purchase price.

All states saw drops in investor lending except for Tasmania and ACT — perhaps reflecting a desire for properties with strong rental returns. Source: SBS News

"I think the fall in new investment will potentially have a flow-on effect to the rental market where rental supply will tighten and landlords will have more scope to put up rents," Kusher said, though he noted there wasn't evidence of that happening "just yet".

Both experts hesitate to call this a permanent retreat for investors.

"It is likely that this won't be the case forever," Redman said.

"Once yields return to more attractive levels, we would expect investors to return to the market at a new equilibrium," he said.

"In the short term in particular, there will probably be a higher proportion of owner-occupier purchases in the market until we see yields rebalance and investor sentiment return ... [separately] the structural undersupply of dwellings means prices will continue to increase over the long run, albeit more modestly than recent price growth."

Kusher says at least two to three quarters of data will be needed before drawing any meaningful conclusions, meaning the next quarterly release will be a better indication of investor behaviour as it will be the first to reflect a full three months under the new environment.

A win for first-home buyers?

The policy case for the tax changes rested on the idea that pushing investors out would clear space for first-home buyers.

But the numbers haven't quite shown that yet, Kusher says, adding that two things may be happening.

First-home buyers do not directly replace all the investors who have retreated — first-home buyers do not entirely fill the gap as they are a smaller group of buyers than investors. Secondly, first-home buyers, like investors, are also in a “wait and see” mode.

"There's an assumption that if you don't have an investor, you have a first-home buyer. That's not always the case. Not everyone that's currently renting is in a position to buy a home,” Kusher said.

Investors make up about 40 per cent of the residential market, but first-home buyers have never been that large a group, he added.

"So, if you're discouraging investors and trying to encourage first-time buyers, you're probably going to struggle to see an uplift in first-home buyer lending offset the weakness in investor lending — and that's certainly what we've seen,” Kusher said.

He notes that some first-home buyers may be falling into a "trap" of trying to time a falling market but warns “picking the bottom of the market” is incredibly difficult.

"I think what these [tax] changes have done more than anything else is just damaged sentiment around the housing market," he said.

title: Australia news LIVE: Labor signs off on gambling reform deal with Coalition; Trump threatens to bomb Oman as US-Iran war agreement expires
text:
Labor has crunched the parliamentary timetable to push through proposed laws on gambling advertising, reducing spending on the NDIS, and forcing tech giants to pay for news.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor appears to have struck a deal with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to support Labor’s NDIS cuts, which save more than $35 billion over four years and angered the disability sector.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during question time last month. Alex Ellinghausen

In exchange, Labor will act more quickly on its pledge to clean up an unintended consequence from its property tax changes causing divorcees or spouses of deceased people to lose grandfathered negative gearing and capital gains concessions. Labor previously argued the change would take months, until Taylor demanded a quicker resolution yesterday.

Labor and the Coalition agreed to condense debate on a gambling crackdown and push the bill to the Senate by tomorrow morning, allowing it to pass the parliament this week.

Labor’s caucus signed off on changes that would create an opt-out register for gambling advertising. Gambling firms will pay for the new register themselves. Inducements to bet will also be cut back. Labor has also shifted from 6am to 5am the start time or a cap of three ads per hour.

Some Coalition MPs want the clampdown on ads to go further. Backbenchers Andrew Wallace, Paul Scarr and Nationals frontbencher Pat Conaghan have all reserved their right to vote against the bill, which Taylor has negotiated with Albanese for a week.

title: Revealed: The $129m plan to bulldoze a Sydney sporting field for homes
text:

NationalNSWCity life Revealed: The $129m plan to bulldoze a Sydney sporting field for homes David Barwell August 18, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After years of political wrangling, community protests and a failed campaign to preserve one of Sydney’s long-held suburban sporting grounds, residents have been given their clearest picture yet of a proposed transformation of TG Millner Reserve in Marsfield. A $128.9 million plan lodged with Ryde Council this week shows the former spiritual home of Eastwood Rugby Club is one step closer to being bulldozed to make way for a 106-home housing estate. A concept image of the $129 million redevelopment of the site. The proposal marks a major milestone in a bitter battle that has pitted Ryde Council against the NSW government, divided residents and highlighted growing tensions between housing growth and the increasing pressure on sporting fields across Sydney. The plans by TGM Developer Pty Ltd, a consortium involving property developer Winston Langley and the Abadeen Group, represent a significant departure from an earlier proposal for 132 seniors housing dwellings on the site. Instead, the revised plan would deliver 106 private homes ranging from three to five bedrooms.

Advertisement

The six-hectare development would involve the demolition of the district-grade rugby field, grandstand, North Ryde RSL Sports Club and Guardian Childcare Marsfield, a 78-place centre operating within the site. It is understood families were informed in January that the centre would cease operating in December 2026 and families would be supported to transition to alternative nearby services. Development plans lodged with the council describe the project as a “garden neighbourhood” designed to balance housing supply with open space. The proposal includes a new public park and the planting of 456 trees, offsetting the loss of 253 existing trees that would be removed during construction works. The sports ground is a step closer to being transformed into homes. The unveiling of the plans is the latest chapter in the fraught history of the site, which has served as the home of Eastwood Rugby and generations of its members and supporters since 1950. In more recent decades, however, the club has faced increasing financial pressures as participation in local rugby union declined and the club’s players, members and sponsors increasingly shifted towards Sydney’s rapidly growing north-west.

Advertisement

Planning documents to the council stated suburban development around the fields has also created ongoing conflicts over parking, lighting and match-day crowds, limiting opportunities to expand operations. As ageing facilities became increasingly expensive to maintain, Eastwood Rugby and North Ryde RSL – which acquired the site in 2017 – ultimately opted to relocate to a new Centre of Excellence at Fred Caterson Reserve, almost 20 kilometres away in Castle Hill. Ryde Council has consistently opposed any redevelopment of the site. Janie Barrett To help fund the move, TG Millner Reserve was sold to TGM Landowner Pty Ltd in December last year. Ryde Council has consistently opposed residential development of the site, arguing the loss of TG Millner would worsen a shortage of sporting fields as housing development accelerates across surrounding suburbs including Macquarie Park and North Ryde.

Advertisement

Between 2018 and 2020, the council explored heritage listing the site but abandoned the effort after independent studies found it lacked sufficient local heritage significance. It later set aside $15 million and sought state approval to compulsorily acquire the land. However, the bid collapsed when Local Government Minister Ron Hoenig rejected the request, citing concerns about the council’s ability to fund both the purchase and ongoing maintenance of the site. A concept image of the development. The council has continued to campaign against the redevelopment. Last month, Mayor Trenton Brown described TG Millner as critical community infrastructure and launched a $40,000 council-funded campaign urging the community to support efforts to save the fields and pressure Planning Minister Paul Scully to reject the rezoning. But councillor Lyndal Howison, who is Labor’s candidate for Ryde at next year’s state election, warned the campaign risked creating false hope, noting the Sydney North Planning Panel had already determined the proposal had strategic merit and should proceed through the planning system.

Advertisement

In its 2025 ruling, the panel found the redevelopment would help deliver much-needed “missing middle” housing – a decision welcomed by North Ryde RSL chief executive Joe Kelly, who said redevelopment would help secure the long-term future of both the RSL and Eastwood Rugby. Ryde Mayor Trenton Brown. Sam Mooy In a statement, Winston Langley executive director David Hynes said: “Ryde Council has opposed the proposal at every stage and has spent over $100,000 of ratepayers’ money and passed over a dozen mayoral minutes seeking to devalue the privately-owned land, confuse the public, and bleed the community clubs into submission.” “Winston Langley and Abadeen are committed to delivering a project that provides meaningful community benefits through 106 low-rise homes for families and extensive publicly accessible open space,” he said. Ryde state Liberal MP Jordan Lane has backed the council’s renewed campaign and accused the NSW government of failing to properly support the reserve.

The Australian sharemarket was a mixed bag in early trade on Tuesday, as jumps by heavyweights BHP and CSL following their profit results offset falls in banking, tech and consumer stocks over rising inflation concerns as hopes for a deal to end the Iran war are fading. The S&P/ASX 200 was up just 4.9 points, or less than 0.1 per cent, at 9078.10 as of 10.44am AEST, with seven of its 11 industry sectors in the red. The local bourse lost 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.03¢. Wall Street opened the week with more losses. Bloomberg BHP, the world’s biggest mining company and the biggest stock on the ASX, jumped 3.6 per cent after saying a copper bonanza is fuelling a jump in revenue and profits, and announced its biggest dividend payout in four years. The resources giant reported a 9 per cent lift in full-year profit to $US9.8 billion ($13.8 billion) as revenues jumped 15 per cent to $US58.8 billion as the red metal’s price hits record highs and shortages of concentrates and other feedstocks in China crimp output from its smelters.

BHP will pay a final dividend of US99¢ per share, taking its full-year payout to $US1.72 a share, up from $US1.10 in the previous year. The $US8.7 billion total payout for the year is the biggest dividend bonanza for BHP’s shareholders in four years. Its smaller rivals Rio Tinto and Fortescue were up 0.4 per cent and 1.2 per cent, respectively. Shares in gold miner Ausgold skyrocketed 24 per cent after the company said it agreed to be taken over by Canada’s OceanaGold for $776 million. Related Article Earnings season ‘Copper is the engine’: Red metal bonanza fuels BHP’s $14b profit Meanwhile, Australia’s biggest health-care company CSL soared 14.8 per cent despite posting a net loss of $US2.6 billion due to restructuring costs and impairments. Revenue slid 1 per cent to $US15.8 billion, beating the $US15.4 billion analyst estimate. The blood giant said it would return to underlying net profit growth of about 5 per cent at constant currency for fiscal 2027, as it pushes ahead with a sweeping restructuring. The results were consistent with CSL’s May update and included $US800 million of one-time pretax restructuring costs and $US7.1 billion of pretax impairments, the company said.

Advertisement

Energy stocks also advanced, with local oil and gas giants Woodside and Santos up 0.6 per cent and 0.4 per cent, respectively, as the price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, climbed again as prospects for peace in the Middle East dimmed, reviving concerns that prolonged geopolitical tensions may threaten supplies and keep energy costs elevated. Brent edged higher to $US91.15 a barrel after President Donald Trump said he wasn’t interested in extending the expiring agreement with Iran and fighting flared anew in Lebanon. Its price has been careening back and forth because of uncertainty about what the war with Iran will do. Last month alone, Brent zigzagged between $US72 and US102 as hopes rose and fell that the US and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. Meanwhile, financial stocks - which make up about a third of the ASX - struggled, with all big four banks in the red this morning. CBA fell 1.4 per cent, National Australia Bank dropped 1.2 per cent, Westpac shed 1.5 per cent and ANZ Bank lost 1.6 per cent. Cyclical stocks dependent on economic growth, strong consumer demand and affordable borrowing costs also declined, with retail conglomerate Wesfarmers down 1.2 per cent, supermarket giants Woolworths and Coles down 1.9 per cent and 1.5 per cent, respectively, and tech stocks such as Xero (down 1.2 per cent), Technology One (down 1.4 per cent) and Life 360 (down 4.4 per cent) in the red. On Wall Street overnight, the S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent but remains near its all-time high set Thursday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.3 per cent. Wall Street’s losses solidified in the afternoon when oil prices accelerated upward.

Related Article Exclusive

James Packer James Packer’s bets on AI pay off after sell-down in gaming shares Wall Street has run to records in large part because profits are booming for US companies. Those in the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver growth of roughly 50 per cent for earnings per share in the spring from a year earlier, according to FactSet. That’s much better than analysts expected and would be the best since five years ago, when the economy was erupting out of the chasm created by the COVID pandemic. Nearly all the companies in the S&P 500 have turned in their profit reports for the Northern hemisphere spring. Still to come are big retailers, including reports this week from Home Depot, Target and Walmart. They’re facing pressure. Their customers’ incomes may be turning iffier after US employers surprisingly cut more jobs last month than they added. At the same time, their customers are continuing to see bills rise quickly as inflation remains much higher than anyone would like. A report last week said that shoppers surprisingly spent less at US retailers last month than in June, and CEOs for retailers could give colour this week on what they’re seeing.

In the bond market, Treasury yields ticked higher following their own big recent moves. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.72 per cent from 4.68 per cent late on Friday following a report showing stronger-than-expected growth in manufacturing in New York state. The 10-year yield has shot up from 3.97 per cent before the war with Iran, largely because higher oil prices raised the pressure on inflation and upped the probability that the Federal Reserve will have to hike interest rates. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy and making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. The average long-term US mortgage rate has already jumped near its highest level in a year because of the rise in the 10-year Treasury yield. Reports last week, though, showed that inflation last month was not as bad as earlier in the summer. That raised hopes that the Fed could wait until later in the year before having to decide whether to raise its main interest rate. Usually around this time of year, anticipation is building on Wall Street to hear from the head of the Federal Reserve about where interest rates may be heading. But the Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, may give little insight at this year’s economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, at the end of this month, according to Thierry Wizman, a strategist at Macquarie Group.

title: Billions of views is just the start – meet the Aussie content creators building global empires
text:

CultureMoviesYouTube Billions of views is just the start – meet the Aussie content creators building global empires Garry Maddox August 18, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Wendy Huang was working as an accountant until the make-up and beauty tutorials she started making for YouTube in 2013 opened up a spectacular new career. The thousands of videos she has created since then for her channels on the platform, including life hacks, crafts and music videos, have attracted more than 13 million subscribers around the world and have been viewed 1.9 billion times. “I had no idea you could make money. I had no idea it was a career path”: Wendy Huang, aka YouTube creator Wengie. Wendy Huang “It was very interactive and fun,” Huang, 40, said of her early days building an online community from her bedroom in Sydney. “I had no idea you could make money. I had no idea it was a career path. I had absolutely no clue.” Known online as Wengie, her nickname, the Chinese-Australian digital creator and musician has also released singles in English, Mandarin, Korean, Filipino and Hindi.

Advertisement

At her most prolific, Huang was creating 25 videos a week, earning a percentage of the revenue from the ads that YouTube ran. “I was making six figures a month at one point so it was pretty lucrative,” she said. Related Article Horror The algorithm of fear: How YouTubers became the new masters of horror Now Huang is among 10 YouTube creators who are being honoured by the National Film and Sound Archive for their contribution to the country’s cultural heritage. At an event at Parliament House in Canberra on Monday evening, the archive announced that 300 of these creators’ videos, oral histories and related material would be added to its audiovisual collection. YouTube creators are increasingly jumping to mainstream cinema success, including Australia’s Danny and Michael Philippou (Talk To Me, Bring Her Back) and Michael Shanks (Together), Sweden’s David F. Sandberg (Shazam! Fury of the Gods) and Americans Bo Burnham (Eighth Grade), Dan Trachtenberg (10 Cloverfield Lane), Curry Barker (Obsession) and Kane Parsons (Backrooms).

Advertisement

Despite huge viewing numbers, videos on the free platform tend to be regarded as ephemeral and niche. “Culture is always shaped by people who, in their day, are ephemeral and niche,” archive chief executive Patrick McIntyre said. “They’re still critical to collect for an understanding of culture across time.” The best-known of the archive’s creators are maths teacher Eddie Woo (2 million subscribers, 188 million views) and musician Tash Sultana (1.3 million subscribers, 424 million views). But the Creator Capsule also recognises the phenomenal success of little-known Thai-Australian brothers Kevin and Luke Lerdwichagul, who created the animation studio Glitch Productions (23 million subscribers, 3.9 billion views). Brothers Luke and Kevin Lerdwichagul, left to right, who are the creators of the YouTube animation channel Glitch. National Film and Sound Archive

Advertisement

They have gone from making videos in their bedroom to employing about 200 people full-time to create six animated shows, including The Amazing Digital Circus and Murder Drones, in their main studio in Parramatta and others including Melbourne CBD, Brisbane and the ACT. Kevin, 32, said the brothers played a lot of video games out the back of their parents’ fruit and vegetable shop in Bondi Junction when they were growing up. That led to Luke, now 27, posting videos online that had him voicing characters over captures of gaming screens about 2010. By the time Luke was finishing high school, he had almost a million subscribers. Kevin, who had studied software engineering at uni, joined him to write and produce these videos. Maths teacher Eddie Woo is one of 10 YouTube creators being honoured by the National Film and Sound Archive in Canberra. Rhett Wymann “We loved watching anime,” Kevin said. “We always wanted to get into animation so we were like, ‘okay, let’s just give it a go’.”

Who would have thought that with every interaction Nathan Cleary had with a young Isaiya Katoa, he would be unknowingly masterminding the Dolphins’ historic maiden finals campaign? As Cleary orchestrated the early days of Penrith’s four-straight premierships, Katoa bided his time and watched how the man now regarded as the NRL’s best player went about his business. At the centre of the program is a key rule that dictates how much they can save, and it all comes down to size.

The bigger the battery, the bigger the discount.

Discounts will be around 30 to 40 per cent on battery installation when it's packaged with a new solar system.

The ultimate goal is to get businesses to store more solar energy, so they can slash their power bills.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers during Question Time at Parliament House in Canberra. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman

Labor, which needs the Coalition's support to pass the reforms through the upper house, had signalled a willingness to accelerate the passage of the tax amendments through parliament.

Earlier, Mr Chalmers told reporters at Parliament House no issues had been raised with the draft legislation for the next tranche of tax reform laws, which includes an amendment to protect those acquiring a property after death or divorce, released two weeks ago.

title: Virgin Australia passenger 'humiliated' after being kicked off flight by crew
text:
A passenger on board a Virgin plane from Sydney to Adelaide says he was left 'angry and upset' after being forced off the flight before takeoff.

Shane Hryhorec, a wheelchair user and disability advocate, told Yahoo News he has never felt more "humiliated" by airline staff than he did on the scheduled flight on Monday.

Shane was travelling with his service dog and a Smart Drive, a motorised power-assist device that attaches to the back of a manual wheelchair.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I'm an incomplete quadriplegic, which means I've got some limited upper body strength, and I have a power assist called a SmartDrive, which allows me to be independent," he explained.

Because of its size, he said it doesn't easily fit under the seat in front of him. Previously, when he travelled, he could put it in the overhead locker.

During his flight on Monday, he learned of a rule change that meant he could no longer do this. Instead, staff were allegedly making him place the large device under his seat.

But a problem arose because the seat he was assigned by the airline lacked space due to an obstruction, he said.

Shane was told to place his SmartDrive device under the seat in front of him, but there was no space due to an obstruction (left). (Shane Hryhorec)

Why is Virgin's rule change so problematic?

Shane said he requested a seat change to accommodate himself, his service dog, and his device. But staff allegedly refused.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I've sat in that same seat for three other flights on this trip, and I did the same thing every time with absolutely no issues," he said.

"All of a sudden it's an issue, and the way that the airline dealt with it was absolutely appalling and disgusting, humiliating, and it shouldn't be happening in the year 2026."

"This new rule has been implemented by Virgin and the airlines without actually thinking about the implications for people with disabilities," he said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The wheelchair user said airline staff would not budge and ultimately kicked him off the plane to avoid any further delays.

"It made me feel so humiliated, so small, so degraded, and it actually just made me feel sick," he told Yahoo on Tuesday.

Shane was placed on the next flight and given three seats to accommodate his service dog and ample under-seat storage for the device. (Shane Hryhorec)

"I was so embarrassed because the plane was full, I was holding up the plane, and the airline made me feel like I was a criminal."

"It made me feel like I was breaking the rules. But it was quite the opposite. I wanted to follow the rules, but the rules were non-negotiable with the restrictions that were placed upon me by the airline," he continued.

"The way that the crew spoke to me was absolutely disgusting. You don't talk to any person in that way.

"It just shows that Virgin truly doesn't care about people with disabilities".

Virgin 'reviewing the circumstances' of passenger's experience

It's understood the ordeal lasted about 30 minutes before the decision to move Shane to an alternative flight was made.

On the next flight, Shane was able to place the device inside a bag under the seat. (Shane Hryhorec)

"Virgin Australia remains committed to providing an accessible and inclusive travel experience for all our guests," a Virgin Australia spokesperson told Yahoo News.

"While the safety of our guests and crew is always our highest priority, we are reviewing the circumstances of yesterday's experience to understand whether there are opportunities to better identify specific seating or stowage requirements in advance and how our teams can support guests in similar circumstances."

According to Virgin, battery-powered mobility aids must be carried and stowed in accordance with aviation safety and Virgin Australia requirements.

Their website provides guidance on travelling with battery-powered mobility aids, including battery types, preparation requirements and cabin carriage requirements.

Virgin said it has reached out to Mr Hryhorec to find out more about his experience.

"We are reviewing the circumstances that led to this unfortunate outcome for one of our guests," the spokesperson said.
